articles.body: Americas Dry Cargo Brazilian soybean exports smash records Sam Chambers November 12, 2026 0 5 1 minute read Norden Norden Brazilian soybean exports have smashed all previous records, with shipments during the first ten months of 2026 already exceeding the whole of last year’s total, providing a significant boost to dry bulk shipping demand, primarily panamaxes and supramaxes. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers shows seaborne soybean exports reached 108.4m tonnes between January and October, an increase of 7.9%, or 7.9m tonnes, compared with the same period last year. The ten-month total was also 600,000 tonnes higher than shipments during the whole of 2025. The second quarter proved particularly strong, with exports climbing 10.3% to 44.9m tonnes, while third-quarter volumes increased 8.1% to 29.7m tonnes. October shipments reached 6.5m tonnes, up 2.4% year-on-year, although volumes declined almost 14% from September as the previous harvest season wound down. Brazilian government customs data independently confirms the record-breaking trend, although its figures differ slightly from Ursa’s vessel-tracking estimates. Official exports reached 106.5m tonnes through October, up 5.9% year-on-year, generating $46bn in export revenue. The outlook suggests further records could follow. The US Department of Agriculture’s latest forecasts put Brazil’s 2026/27 soybean harvest at 186m tonnes, with exports projected to reach 118m tonnes. The growth is being driven primarily by increased acreage rather than higher yields, with harvested area forecast to expand to 50m hectares. Brazil’s own crop agency, Conab, is more conservative, projecting production of approximately 181.6m tonnes. With China remaining the dominant destination for Brazilian soybeans, further export growth has the potential to support tonne-mile demand well into 2027, something that will be under the microscope when the Agri-Commodities panel reconvenes on April 28 at Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference. articles.title: HMM operating profit surges 370% in third quarter
articles.summary: South Korean container shipping company HMM reported a sharp increase in earnings for the third quarter of 2026, with operating profit rising 370% year-on-year amid improvements in operational efficiency and profitability across its shipping businesses. The carrier recorded consolidated revenue of KRW 4.13 trillion...
articles.body: South Korean container shipping company HMM reported a sharp increase in earnings for the third quarter of 2026, with operating profit rising 370% year-on-year amid improvements in operational efficiency and profitability across its shipping businesses. The carrier recorded consolidated revenue of KRW 4.13 trillion during the quarter, up 52% from KRW 2.71 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025. Operating profit climbed to KRW 1.40 trillion from KRW 297 billion a year earlier, while net profit increased 405% to KRW 1.54 trillion, compared with KRW 304 billion in the third quarter of 2025. The company reported an operating profit margin of approximately 34%, reflecting its ongoing focus on cost optimisation and efficient fleet operations. Compared with the second quarter of 2026, revenue increased by 21%, while operating profit rose by 294% and net profit advanced by 273%. Container division strengthens nine-month earnings HMM’s container shipping division recorded operating profit of KRW 1.64 trillion during the first nine months of 2026, representing a 55.3% increase compared with the same period last year. According to the company, the division focused on expanding its shipping network and securing higher-yield cargo through its hub-and-spoke strategy. HMM said these operational measures supported profitability despite continued global uncertainty, including geopolitical risks in the Middle East and natural disasters affecting major ports. Across the Group, revenue for the first nine months reached KRW 10.25 trillion, an increase of 25% from KRW 8.18 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025. Cumulative operating profit rose 76% to KRW 2.02 trillion, compared with KRW 1.14 trillion a year earlier, while net profit increased 52% to KRW 2.30 trillion. Bulk shipping growth supports diversification HMM’s bulk shipping division also delivered stronger results during the nine-month period, with operating profit increasing 418.5% year-on-year to KRW 378 billion. The segment’s contribution to total operating profit rose from 6.4% to 18.8%, reflecting the growing importance of the company’s non-container shipping activities. HMM attributed the bulk division’s performance to its long-term contracts, which helped maintain a stable revenue base amid market volatility. The company is also continuing to diversify its fleet beyond dry bulk carriers and tankers, expanding into pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs), gas carriers and multipurpose vessels (MPVs). The latest results highlight HMM’s improved earnings performance across both its container and bulk shipping businesses, with the container division remaining the largest contributor to operating profit.

Operating profit climbed to KRW 1.40 trillion from KRW 297 billion a year earlier, while net profit increased 405% to KRW 1.54 trillion, compared with KRW 304 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd nearly doubles Q3 EBITDA and raises 2026 outlook
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd reported a sharp improvement in third-quarter earnings in 2026, supported by higher freight rates and strong vessel utilisation, while upgrading its full-year earnings outlook amid continued favourable market conditions. The German container shipping company recorded Group EBITDA of US$1.73 billion in the...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd reported a sharp improvement in third-quarter earnings in 2026, supported by higher freight rates and strong vessel utilisation, while upgrading its full-year earnings outlook amid continued favourable market conditions. The German container shipping company recorded Group EBITDA of US$1.73 billion in the third quarter, nearly double the US$866 million reported in the same period last year. Group EBIT increased to US$1.09 billion from US$228 million, while net profit climbed to US$999 million from US$172 million. Group revenue reached US$6.88 billion, compared with US$5.46 billion in the third quarter of 2025. The improvement was primarily driven by higher freight rates in the Liner Shipping segment, although geopolitical tensions and weather-related disruptions continued to put pressure on operating costs. Higher freight rates support liner shipping earnings Hapag-Lloyd’s average freight rate increased by approximately 28% year-on-year to US$1,808 per TEU, compared with US$1,413 per TEU in the third quarter of 2025. Transport volumes remained broadly stable at 3.38 million TEU, slightly below the 3.40 million TEU recorded a year earlier. Liner Shipping revenue rose to US$6.72 billion, while segment EBITDA increased to US$1.67 billion from US$836 million. Operating profit reached US$1.05 billion, compared with US$219 million in the previous year. Despite the improved earnings, the carrier reported continued pressure on unit costs due to the conflict in the Middle East and weather-related operational disruptions. Meanwhile, Hapag-Lloyd’s Terminal & Infrastructure segment also recorded growth, with quarterly revenue increasing to US$197 million from US$131 million a year earlier. Segment EBITDA rose to US$56 million from US$30 million, while EBIT increased to US$34 million from US$9 million. The company attributed the improvement to investments in terminal capacity and stronger performance at its Latin American terminals. Hapag-Lloyd raises full-year earnings guidance Following the stronger third-quarter performance and continued favourable spot freight rates, Hapag-Lloyd’s Executive Board decided on 11 November to raise its earnings forecast for 2026. The company now expects Group EBITDA of between US$4.6 billion and US$5.0 billion, with Group EBIT projected at US$2.0 billion to US$2.4 billion. Hapag-Lloyd said its fourth-quarter performance was developing better than previously anticipated, although the outlook remains subject to considerable uncertainty due to volatile freight rates and geopolitical developments. “We delivered a strong third quarter, driven by significantly higher spot rates, robust demand and high capacity utilization,” said Rolf Habben Jansen, CEO of Hapag-Lloyd. Despite the strong quarterly recovery, the company’s nine-month results presented a more mixed picture. Group EBITDA for the first nine months increased to US$3.05 billion from US$2.79 billion a year earlier, while EBIT rose to US$1.10 billion from US$905 million. However, cumulative Group profit declined to US$827 million from US$946 million in the corresponding period of 2025. The figures underline the impact of the third-quarter freight rate recovery on the carrier’s profitability, while highlighting the continued influence of operating costs and market volatility on its broader annual performance.

Group EBIT increased to US$1.09 billion from US$228 million, while net profit climbed to US$999 million from US$172 million.

articles.title: Maersk hit by fresh cyber breach
articles.summary: Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed another cybersecurity breach after hackers gained access to an older IT system and extracted data, nearly a decade after the devastating NotPetya attack that cost the company up to $300m. The Copenhagen-headquartered group said on Wednesday that the incident...
articles.body: Containers Europe Maersk hit by fresh cyber breach Adis Ajdin November 12, 2026 0 1,231 1 minute read Cydome Cydome Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed another cybersecurity breach after hackers gained access to an older IT system and extracted data, nearly a decade after the devastating NotPetya attack that cost the company up to $300m. The Copenhagen-headquartered group said on Wednesday that the incident involved a local legacy system inherited through a previous acquisition. Maersk’s cybersecurity team launched an investigation after discovering the intrusion and has taken steps to secure the affected system.”Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed,” the company said. The carrier said the breach appeared to be confined to the legacy system, with no indication that other Maersk systems or those belonging to customers and partners connected through APIs and electronic data interchange (EDI) had been compromised. The company added that it does not expect disruption to customer operations, with its digital booking and shipment management platforms continuing to operate normally. Maersk has not identified the acquired business involved, disclosed what data was extracted or named those responsible for the intrusion. The announcement follows separate claims by a hacker group calling itself WhiteArmor that it had obtained around 100 GB of logistics data from a platform associated with LF Logistics, the Hong Kong-based logistics business Maersk acquired for $3.6bn in 2022. The group has reportedly demanded $5m in bitcoin. The claims remain unverified, and Maersk has not confirmed any connection between the alleged theft and the incident it is investigating. The latest breach brings back memories of June 2017, when the NotPetya malware attack crippled Maersk’s IT infrastructure and disrupted container shipping and terminal operations worldwide. The Danish group subsequently put the financial damage at between $250m and $300m, making it one of the costliest cyber incidents in shipping history. articles.body: Bunkering Bunker prices plunge 20% Sam Chambers November 12, 2026 0 249 1 minute read Bunker prices have plunged by as much as 20% in less than two weeks as hopes of an easing of the Iran conflict send oil markets tumbling, offering shipowners some relief from what is still expected to be the most expensive year for marine fuel on record. Singapore very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) was assessed by Ship & Bunker at $814.50 a tonne yesterday, down from $1,019.50 on October 30, a drop of $205, or 20.1%. The retreat represents a saving of $615,000 on a 3,000-tonne bunker stem compared with the end of last month. The price reversal has been equally dramatic elsewhere. Ship & Bunker’s 20-port global VLSFO average has fallen from $999 a tonne on October 30 to $842 yesterday, a decline of 15.7%. In Fujairah, VLSFO was assessed at $813.50 yesterday, while Rotterdam was considerably cheaper at $710. The sharp correction follows growing optimism that the conflict with Iran could be heading towards a diplomatic resolution, alongside recovering Middle Eastern oil flows. Brent crude briefly fell below $90 a barrel on Tuesday, its lowest level since late August, although uncertainty surrounding peace negotiations continues to generate considerable volatility. Splash reported on November 3 that Singapore VLSFO had climbed back above $1,000 a tonne for the first time since March, with the Iran conflict having almost doubled bunker prices since February. Despite the latest retreat, Singapore fuel remains approximately 56% more expensive than immediately before the war began on February 28. Meanwhile, Clarksons Research has put shipping’s total bunker bill this year at a record $220bn. Speaking at the IBIA Annual Convention in New York yesterday, Clarksons Research managing director Steve Gordon estimated the global bunker market at 290m tonnes annually. Fuel demand is rising again despite modern ships being around 50% more efficient than vessels built 15 years ago. The explanation lies partly in longer voyages caused by geopolitical disruption. Clarksons expects tonne-mile demand to rise by around 1% to 1.5% this year, with average shipping distances having increased approximately 10% during the current decade. articles.title: Geneva Dry: Belships’ Ivar Hansson Myklebust on China’s changing commodities role
articles.summary: Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chair and CEO of Norway’s Belships, believes the shipping industry continues to underestimate the growth potential of developing economies. Ahead of his appearance at Geneva Dry 2027, he discusses China’s changing trading patterns, fleet supply and the opportunities emerging across minor...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Maritime CEO Geneva Dry: Belships’ Ivar Hansson Myklebust on China’s changing commodities role Splash November 12, 2026 0 452 2 minutes read Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chair and CEO of Norway’s Belships, believes the shipping industry continues to underestimate the growth potential of developing economies. Ahead of his appearance at Geneva Dry 2027, he discusses China’s changing trading patterns, fleet supply and the opportunities emerging across minor bulks. A changing China, resilient emerging economies and a relatively predictable fleet supply picture will be among the biggest themes shaping dry bulk shipping when the industry gathers in Geneva next April, according to Ivar Hansson Myklebust. The Belships chief is cautiously optimistic about the outlook for minor bulks, arguing that developing economies continue to generate more trade than many shipping forecasts anticipate. “We tend to underestimate both the economic growth and physical trade volumes originating to and from developing countries,” Myklebust says. He believes this trend will continue to support the handysize and supramax markets. “The positive development in trade volumes for most minor bulks is due to this development, and on the balance I think this effect will be with us for some time.” Myklebust brings considerable industry experience to the discussion. Before joining Belships, he headed OMP Management and held senior leadership positions at Höegh Autoliners and Norden. He also chaired Gram Car Carriers until its acquisition by MSC. Looking ahead to Geneva Dry, he identifies the balance between future fleet supply and underlying demand as a central issue. “We have uncertainties galore regarding demand development now, while the fleet demographics are pretty well-known for the next three to four years,” he observes. Geopolitical disruption remains another major concern, particularly following the deadly attacks on merchant shipping in the Black Sea and Arabian Gulf “I sincerely hope that the hostilities that have caused tragic seafarer casualties both in the Black Sea and the Arabian Gulf have come to an end or at least calmed down significantly by then. Fingers crossed,” he says. China’s changing role in dry bulk shipping is another development he believes deserves closer attention. “From being an almost sole importer of dry cargoes it has emerged into a large exporter over the last few years, a very interesting development indeed,” he says. The shift is altering demand for geared bulk carriers in the Pacific, adding new dimensions to the traditional trade patterns that have underpinned the sector for decades. Whether China’s growing export role continues will be an important question for owners positioning their fleets. On technology, Myklebust sees opportunities less in revolutionary developments than in improving everyday shipping processes, from maintenance planning to freight collection. Myklebust will join the Minor Bulks panel at Geneva Dry on Wednesday, April 28, alongside Emilie Nourry of Eramet, Malgorzata Gill of Holcim Trading, S.K. Lim of G2 Ocean and Vincenzo Romeo of Nova Marine Carriers. Braemar’s global head of dry research, Derek Langston, will moderate. For Myklebust, the value of Geneva Dry lies in bringing together the different sides of the commodities shipping business. “Hearing the differing views and opinions from key players from the horses’ mouth is always interesting,” he says. “And meeting market participants from all sides of the business is never a waste of time.” Geneva Dry 2027, the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, takes place at the Hotel President Wilson on April 27 and 28 with organisers today unveiling limited special discount rates at the five-star hotel for signed-up delegates. articles.summary: One of the world’s largest shipowners has given its take on where it sees the gas, dry bulk, and tanker markets heading in the coming years. articles.body: Asia Dry Cargo Gas Operations Tankers NYK charts the great reshuffling of global commodity trades Sam Chambers November 12, 2026 0 60 1 minute read NYK NYK One of the world’s largest shipowners has given its take on where it sees the gas, dry bulk, and tanker markets heading in the coming years. The global VLCC fleet will see a significant expansion despite the extraordinary earnings currently being enjoyed by tanker owners, with Japanese shipping giant Nippon Yusen Kaisha (NYK) forecasting the delivery of approximately 290 supertankers between 2026 and 2029. NYK’s research group unveiled its latest shipping market outlook yesterday, predicting that the active VLCC fleet will increase from 909 vessels at the end of 2025 to 1,082 by the end of 2029, a rise of 19%. The forecast assumes a substantial number of ageing vessels will leave the market, but deliveries are expected to be comparable to those witnessed during the shipping boom of the 2000s. NYK’s research also anticipates a fundamental restructuring of global commodity trades over the coming decade. Seaborne iron ore volumes are forecast to decline from 1.65bn tonnes in 2025 to 1.40bn tonnes in 2035 as Chinese steel production contracts. However, increasing shipments from Guinea’s Simandou project are expected to support tonne-mile demand as Atlantic basin cargoes replace some Australian supplies. Coal shipments are forecast to fall from 1.33bn tonnes to 1.04bn tonnes over the same period, with thermal coal accounting for most of the decline.< LNG is heading in the opposite direction, with seaborne volumes expected to climb from 433m tonnes to 622m tonnes by 2035. NYK anticipates LNG tonne-mile demand growing faster than cargo volumes as trading distances increase. India and Southeast Asia are expected to become increasingly important demand centres for energy and commodities as China’s import growth slows. articles.body: Asia Piracy Singapore Strait robbery spike sparks fresh security warning Sam Chambers November 12, 2026 0 185 1 minute read Nicholas Brown Nicholas Brown A sudden resurgence in robberies aboard merchant ships in the Singapore Strait has prompted regional maritime security authorities to issue an urgent warning, with three vessels boarded in nine days and one seafarer injured. The ReCAAP Information Sharing Centre issued an incident alert yesterday following attacks on two bulk carriers and a tanker between November 2 and 10, warning that further incidents are possible. All three robberies occurred in the eastbound lane of the Traffic Separation Scheme, within approximately 3.2 nautical miles of each other. The first incident involved the bulk carrier Star Calypso, boarded at 2125 hrs on November 2. The second, involving the bulk carrier APJ Priti 2, took place late on November 4, followed by an attack on the tanker Salsa in the early hours of November 10. One crewmember sustained injuries during the attacks. Engine spare parts were stolen from two vessels, while nothing was reported missing from the third. The latest incidents bring the number of robberies reported in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore this year to 28. ReCAAP is urging Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore to intensify patrols and surveillance, improve coordination and share intelligence to identify and arrest those responsible. Shipmasters have been advised to maintain heightened vigilance, particularly during darkness, and strengthen preventive measures, including CCTV coverage of potential boarding locations. The organisation is also encouraging vessels to report suspicious activity immediately and use its digital reporting and incident mapping systems when assessing voyage risks. articles.body: Americas Tankers Teekay Tankers doubles down on newbuilds with four-ship deal Adis Ajdin November 12, 2026 0 271 1 minute read Teekay Teekay US-listed Teekay Tankers has ordered four more newbuildings in China and South Korea, lifting its tanker construction programme to six ships worth $525.9m. The Kenneth Hvid-led owner has booked two aframax/LR2 tankers at an unnamed Chinese yard and two suezmaxes at a South Korean shipbuilder, with all four vessels scheduled for delivery in 2030. The Chinese contracts were signed in October, followed by the Korean suezmax order this month. The latter also comes with options for two additional suezmaxes, which would take the company’s newbuilding pipeline to eight vessels if exercised. Neither the yards nor the individual contract prices have been disclosed. Teekay had already secured two suezmax resale newbuildings in South Korea earlier this year, paying a combined $190m for vessels due in 2027. The latest orders lift the company’s firm newbuilding commitments to $525.9m across six ships, with around $475m in construction payments outstanding. The expansion comes amid a wider fleet renewal drive that has seen Teekay sell four older tankers for $211m so far this year, booking gains of $77.8m. The owner has also acquired or agreed to acquire four secondhand vessels for a combined $190.3m. Teekay entered the latest investment round with a sizeable cash cushion, reporting $1.42bn in cash and short-term investments at the end of September and no debt. The latest fleet investments come during an extraordinary run for the tanker market. Teekay said its fourth-quarter spot bookings to date averaged $272,000 per day for suezmaxes and $208,300 per day for aframax/LR2 vessels, with chief executive Kenneth Hvid pointing to the potential for record full-year results. The company has also made a move back into the MR product tanker segment after a decade away, agreeing in September to acquire a 2020-built South Korean vessel for delivery by mid-January 2027. Shipbroking sources have linked the acquisition to a disposal by Singapore’s Pacific Carriers, although Teekay has not identified the vessel or its seller. The deal marks a return to a sector Teekay exited in late 2016, when it agreed to sell its last remaining MR tanker. articles.body: Agility Global reported a 22% increase in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, supported by growth across its aviation services, fuel logistics and industrial real estate operations. The Abu Dhabi-listed logistics group generated revenue of US$1.60 billion, compared with US$1.31 billion in the same period last year. However, EBITDA declined 3% to US$208 million, while EBIT decreased slightly to US$125 million. Earnings from the group’s controlled businesses performed more strongly, with EBIT increasing 21% to US$128 million. For the first nine months of 2026, Agility recorded revenue of US$4.52 billion, up 24% year on year. EBIT increased 11% to US$350 million. Logistics parks and operating businesses support growth Agility Logistics Parks reported a 49% increase in quarterly revenue to US$21 million, while EBIT rose 58% to US$17 million. Saudi Arabia remained the primary driver of growth as newly completed logistics facilities began generating income. Higher occupancy levels in Africa also contributed to the improvement. The company is progressing with approximately 82,000 square metres of new facilities scheduled for delivery during 2026 and early 2027, including projects already completed. Its owned and leased land bank reached approximately 4.5 million square metres, increasing to 6.1 million square metres when joint venture holdings are included. Meanwhile, Tristar, Agility’s fuel logistics business, recorded revenue growth of 24% to US$419 million. Its quarterly EBIT increased 23% to US$36 million. Menzies Aviation, the group’s largest operating business, generated US$974 million in revenue, representing a 22% annual increase. Air cargo handling volumes rose 13% to 657,000 tonnes. Tarek Sultan, Chairman of Agility, said the group’s operating businesses continued to recover from challenges encountered earlier in the year. He highlighted improved earnings at Menzies, Tristar and Agility Logistics Parks as important contributors to the group’s performance. Agility advances portfolio restructuring and investment strategy Agility is also progressing with changes to its investment portfolio following the agreement announced on 13 October to sell its 65.12% stake in Tristar to India’s Aegis Logistics. The transaction values Tristar at an enterprise value of US$1.5 billion and is expected to close by the end of March 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other conditions. Agility expects to receive consideration of up to US$581 million from the transaction, including deferred and performance-dependent payments. The group also maintains a substantial investment in global freight forwarder DSV. As of 30 September 2026, Agility held approximately 19.3 million DSV shares, representing an ownership stake of around 8.2%. The carrying value of this investment stood at approximately US$3.5 billion, including the collar value. Agility’s Board also approved an interim dividend of US$75 million. The company said its financial position and future capital allocation decisions will reflect its investment priorities, debt reduction objectives and the expected proceeds from the Tristar transaction.

articles.body: DHL Express has begun construction of a new international logistics gateway near Stockholm Arlanda Airport in Sweden, as part of a wider investment programme to strengthen its Nordic and Baltic network. The project, developed in partnership with Slättö through its logistics and light industrial platform Evolv, represents a total investment of more than €55 million. The facility is scheduled to become operational in 2028. Located in Arlanda Stad, the new gateway will provide additional capacity for international express shipments and improve connections between Swedish businesses and DHL Express’ global network. The investment is intended to support growing import and export requirements across industries such as manufacturing, technology, life sciences, automotive and e-commerce. New facility to increase sorting capacity The planned gateway will cover approximately 14,000 square metres and feature an automated sorting system capable of processing up to 6,000 shipments per hour. It will also include 60 direct-loading positions and infrastructure supporting the use of electric delivery vans. According to DHL Express, the facility has been designed to accommodate future growth while improving shipment handling and operational efficiency. Its location near Stockholm Arlanda Airport and major road connections will support the movement of time-sensitive cargo between international air services and domestic distribution networks. Gareth Biggs, Managing Director of DHL Express Sweden, said changes in global trade patterns were increasing demand for reliable international logistics connections. He highlighted the importance of supply chain diversification and the growing requirements of sectors such as industrial technology, advanced manufacturing and life sciences. Thommy Hall, VP Network Operations at DHL Express Sweden, said the new automated infrastructure would provide additional processing capacity while supporting the company’s longer-term operational requirements. DHL Express expands Nordic-Baltic infrastructure The Stockholm project forms part of a broader DHL Express investment programme covering gateway facilities across Northern Europe. Recent projects include a €100 million gateway at Helsinki-Vantaa Airport in Finland and a €24 million facility at Tallinn Airport in Estonia. Together with the new Swedish development, these investments represent approximately €180 million in gateway infrastructure across the Nordic and Baltic markets. The projects are intended to increase regional processing capacity and strengthen connections with DHL Express’ international network, which covers approximately 220 countries and territories. The company expects the additional infrastructure to support future trade growth and provide businesses with greater access to international express services. The Arlanda gateway will also expand DHL Express’ capacity in Sweden as exporters and importers adapt their supply chains to changing market conditions.

The facility is scheduled to become operational in 2028.

articles.title: Shipping’s $95bn fossil fuel bonfire
articles.summary: The shipping industry has spent an estimated $95bn more on fuel since the Hormuz crisis began. That money could have financed wind propulsion across much of the world’s merchant fleet, slashing emissions and reducing exposure to future energy shocks. Gavin Allwright, secretary-general of the International Windship...
articles.body: Bunkering Contributions Environment Operations Regulatory Shipping’s $95bn fossil fuel bonfire Splash November 12, 2026 0 229 2 minutes read Piet Sinke / Maasmond Maritime Piet Sinke / Maasmond Maritime The shipping industry has spent an estimated $95bn more on fuel since the Hormuz crisis began. That money could have financed wind propulsion across much of the world’s merchant fleet, slashing emissions and reducing exposure to future energy shocks. Gavin Allwright, secretary-general of the International Windship Association (IWSA), writes for Splash today. The maritime shipping industry just set $95bn on fire. Over the past nine months, geopolitical turmoil around the Strait of Hormuz has forced the sector to absorb a massive fossil fuel premium. Had that exact capital been invested into free, zero-emission wind propulsion instead of pouring it into volatile oil markets, shipowners would already be saving billions while helping to permanently secure their energy independence. As negotiators head to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) this December, they are drawing red lines over a proposed $11bn-$12bn fund for the Net-Zero Framework. Yet, the industry just handed over nearly eight times that amount to fossil fuel suppliers since late February. This shocking amount represents a massive transfer of wealth out of the maritime sector with absolutely zero return on long-term energy security or commercial resilience. This is my maths. Since the beginning of this recent geopolitical instability, spiking fuel costs drained an extra $340m a day from the industry throughout March alone. With the global average price of Very Low Sulphur Fuel Oil (VLSFO) surging from $500 to $810 per tonne – with other fuels spiking even higher, making the monthly fuel bill skyrocket from $12.5bn to well over $20bn. If the numbers don’t lie, this adds up to a $95bn toll simply because the industry remains dependent on fossil fuels in an increasingly unstable world and extremely volatile markets. That lost capital could have driven vessels’ energy independence instead. Wind propulsion harnesses a globally abundant energy source delivered entirely free at the point of use. For $95bn, between 100,000 and 200,000 wind-assist retrofit systems could have been funded. That is enough to equip half the current global fleet, slash fuel consumption by 5%, and eliminate 45m tonnes of CO2e emissions every single year. Because wind energy is free, those immediate fuel savings would unlock a further $12bn annually, providing the exact capital needed to reinvest in up to 20,000 more systems a year. By 2040, this deployment cycle would have fully paid for itself, putting that initial $95bn back into shipowners’ pockets to fund further decarbonisation. Alternatively, that same cash could have financed 5,000 to 10,000 newbuild primary-wind vessels, fundamentally transforming the sector by cutting fuel use and emissions by up to 80% per ship. Additionally, this evaporated capital could have fully funded a just and equitable transition for the entire maritime workforce. It could have seamlessly financed the retraining of the 600,000 seafarers who will need to operate alternative technologies and new fuels by the mid-2030s. It would have easily covered the initial $300m-$500m needed by the Pacific Blue Shipping Partnership to deliver dozens of primary wind ships to Pacific islands. With $95bn, we could have scaled this further and rolled out similar programs globally, freeing the world’s most vulnerable economies from their expensive fossil fuel dependency. We cannot recover the billions already burned, but we can stop the bleeding. The ongoing geopolitical crises have ruthlessly exposed the devastating cost of climate inaction and fossil fuel reliance. This December, the Net-Zero Framework is up for adoption once again at IMO and would catalyse the rapid scaling of wind technology and help break the cycle. This December in London, we can finally ensure our next major expenditure places the maritime industry squarely on a pathway towards permanent energy independence. articles.title: VIACHAIN and Star Solutions expand onboard connectivity for smart containers
articles.summary: VIACHAIN, an ORBCOMM company, and Star Solutions have formalized a strategic alliance to expand onboard connectivity for smart containers, strengthening cargo monitoring capabilities during ocean voyages. The partnership combines Star Solutions’ private 4G/LTE networks with VIACHAIN’s connected container technology...
articles.body: VIACHAIN, an ORBCOMM company, and Star Solutions have formalized a strategic alliance to expand onboard connectivity for smart containers, strengthening cargo monitoring capabilities during ocean voyages. The partnership combines Star Solutions’ private 4G/LTE networks with VIACHAIN’s connected container technology and CrewView application. The integration will allow compatible containers to exchange operational data through vessel-based communications networks. The two companies already collaborate across hundreds of vessels operated by major shipping lines, supporting hundreds of thousands of smart containers. The new agreement builds on this existing cooperation as carriers increasingly adopt private cellular networks onboard their vessels. Improving cargo visibility during ocean voyages The alliance aims to improve access to container condition data while vessels are at sea, allowing crews to identify operational issues earlier and respond more efficiently. VIACHAIN’s CrewView application supports the monitoring of compatible refrigerated and dry containers. It identifies temperature deviations, power interruptions and other exceptions that may require intervention. By providing crews with more targeted information, the system can reduce reliance on routine physical inspections and help operators prioritize containers requiring immediate attention. The technology also supports cargo protection and crew safety by limiting unnecessary inspections in potentially hazardous areas onboard. VIACHAIN’s connected container technology currently supports approximately 4 million TEU worldwide. Chip Lebovitz, SVP and General Manager of VIACHAIN, said the company’s objective is to make container information accessible and useful throughout ocean voyages. He explained that improved visibility allows crews to spend less time identifying problems and more time addressing them. The latest partnership follows the earlier introduction of ORBCOMM’s CrewView container monitoring technology , which provides vessel crews with information on container conditions and operational exceptions. Private 4G/LTE networks support connected container operations Star Solutions provides private mobile network infrastructure, including 4G/LTE technology designed for industrial and maritime environments. Through the alliance, shipping lines will have an additional connectivity option for VIACHAIN-enabled containers as they introduce or expand private cellular networks onboard. Jack Mar, CEO of Star Solutions, said private cellular networks help shipping companies make better use of their investments in connected container technology. The companies expect the integration of their communications infrastructure and monitoring applications to support more effective onboard container management. The announcement does not specify additional vessel deployments, new carrier customers or a timetable for further installations. However, the agreement reflects the growing role of onboard communications networks in connecting smart containers with vessel crews and supporting cargo visibility throughout maritime transport operations.

articles.title: Falklands oil dispute heads for international tribunal ruling
articles.summary: The international legal battle over the Sea Lion offshore oil development near the Falkland Islands has moved a step closer to a decision, with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) concluding two days of hearings between Argentina and the United Kingdom. The Hamburg-based tribunal will now...
articles.body: Americas Europe Offshore Falklands oil dispute heads for international tribunal ruling Bojan Lepic November 12, 2026 0 345 1 minute read Falkland Islands Govt Falkland Islands Govt The international legal battle over the Sea Lion offshore oil development near the Falkland Islands has moved a step closer to a decision, with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) concluding two days of hearings between Argentina and the United Kingdom. The Hamburg-based tribunal will now deliberate on Argentina’s request for emergency measures to halt offshore drilling and the installation of production infrastructure linked to the Navitas Petroleum-operated project. A ruling is tentatively scheduled for November 28. During hearings on November 10 and 11, Argentina argued that allowing the project to proceed while the sovereignty dispute remains unresolved would undermine its claimed rights over the surrounding waters and risk environmental damage. The UK rejected the arguments, maintaining that the tribunal lacks jurisdiction over what it considers an underlying sovereignty dispute and that the Falkland Islanders have the right to develop their natural resources. London also argued that Argentina had failed to demonstrate the urgency required for provisional measures, pointing out that drilling is not scheduled to begin before March 21, 2027. Sea Lion, located about 220 km north of the Falklands, is operated by Navitas Petroleum, which holds a 65% interest, while Rockhopper Exploration holds the remaining 35%. The development has been sanctioned, with first oil targeted for 2028. Rockhopper said the proceedings were a state-to-state matter and that it would provide further updates on any implications for the project when appropriate. The hearings follow Argentina’s October application for provisional measures and an earlier Argentine court order seeking to suspend work associated with Sea Lion. The UK has also announced plans to protect companies involved in Falklands-related economic activities from extraterritorial Argentine measures. ITLOS has not issued a suspension order, and the tribunal’s forthcoming decision will address provisional measures rather than a final determination of the sovereignty dispute. articles.title: DH Shipbuilding reports strong nine-month profit growth
articles.summary: South Korea’s DH Shipbuilding reported strong financial results for the first nine months of 2026, supported by higher-value vessel construction and improved shipyard productivity. The shipbuilder recorded cumulative revenue of KRW 990.4 billion and operating profit of KRW 260.6 billion through September, achieving...
articles.body: South Korea’s DH Shipbuilding reported strong financial results for the first nine months of 2026, supported by higher-value vessel construction and improved shipyard productivity. The shipbuilder recorded cumulative revenue of KRW 990.4 billion and operating profit of KRW 260.6 billion through September, achieving an operating profit margin of 26.3%. For the third quarter alone, revenue reached KRW 327.7 billion, while operating profit stood at KRW 82.7 billion. The company attributed its earnings performance to the construction of higher-priced vessels ordered in 2024, alongside productivity improvements from building established vessel designs. DH Shipbuilding has maintained an operating profit margin above 20% for eight consecutive quarters. Margins have also remained above 25% for the last four consecutive quarters. Shipbuilding backlog supports future operations DH Shipbuilding continued to secure new vessel orders during 2026, particularly in the crude oil tanker segment. The company has received orders for 17 Suezmax tankers worth approximately US$1.5 billion this year, exceeding its annual order target by 62%. As of 30 September 2026, its order backlog stood at 35 vessels with a combined value of approximately US$3.3 billion. The existing orderbook provides the shipbuilder with contracted work for the coming years, although the announcement does not specify the delivery schedule for individual vessels. DH Shipbuilding’s nine-month operating profit was equivalent to approximately 89% of the KRW 294.1 billion recorded for the full year of 2025. The company could therefore exceed last year’s annual operating profit if its recent earnings performance continues during the final quarter. However, this remains dependent on the company’s fourth-quarter operating results. New shareholder return policy announced Alongside its earnings update, DH Shipbuilding announced a medium-term shareholder return policy covering the period from 2027 to 2029. Under the plan, the company intends to return at least 30% of its annual consolidated net income to shareholders through cash dividends, share repurchases and share cancellations. The shipbuilder has also approved an additional KRW 10 billion share buyback. Further decisions on dividends, repurchases and cancellations will follow the completion of its financial statements. According to the company, the policy is intended to distribute a portion of future earnings to shareholders while supporting long-term corporate value. The latest results highlight DH Shipbuilding’s continued profitability, supported by its existing vessel backlog and production efficiency improvements.
takeaways: South Korea’s DH Shipbuilding reported strong financial results for the first nine months of 2026, supported by higher-value vessel construction and improved shipyard productivity.
The shipbuilder recorded cumulative revenue of KRW 990.4 billion and operating profit of KRW 260.6 billion through September, achieving an operating profit margin of 26.3%.

articles.body: Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (MOL) reported a sharp increase in containership earnings during the first half of its 2026 fiscal year, supported by stronger profitability at Ocean Network Express (ONE), elevated freight rates and continued capacity constraints across major container shipping routes. The Japanese shipping group’s containership business generated ordinary profit of ¥73.4 billion for the six months ended 30 September 2026, compared with ¥23.9 billion in the corresponding period last year, representing an increase of 206.2%. Revenue from the segment rose 23.4% to ¥54.3 billion, while MOL recorded ¥64.1 billion in equity-method earnings from ONE, reflecting the carrier’s improved financial performance. Strong container market supports earnings According to MOL, container spot freight rates remained elevated, particularly on Asia-North America routes, where sustained cargo demand and congestion at major Asian ports continued to restrict effective vessel capacity. The company said ONE achieved a significant year-on-year improvement in profitability despite higher bunker fuel costs and the suspension of vessel deployments to the Persian Gulf. The stronger performance of its container shipping investment contributed to an increase in MOL’s overall earnings, alongside improvements in dry bulk and energy transportation. However, domestic container terminal operations experienced weaker handling volumes as vessel schedule disruptions caused by congestion at overseas ports affected operations. Meanwhile, MOL reported firm throughput at its overseas container terminal operations, supported by increased import and export activity in Vietnam, partly associated with the relocation of supply chains amid US-China trade tensions. Group profit rises despite higher operating costs MOL recorded consolidated revenue of ¥1.275 trillion during the first half of FY2026, representing a 46.6% increase from ¥869.8 billion a year earlier. Profit attributable to owners of the parent increased 54.3% to ¥179.3 billion, while ordinary profit rose 42.8% to ¥163.6 billion. Operating profit increased more modestly, rising 1.2% to ¥72.7 billion. The year-on-year comparison was affected by changes in the accounting periods of 384 consolidated subsidiaries, which resulted in nine months of their financial results being included in the current reporting period. For the containership segment specifically, the accounting adjustment increased reported revenue by approximately ¥8.8 billion and segment profit by ¥437 million. The company also faced substantially higher fuel costs, with average bunker prices increasing to US$865 per metric tonne from US$546 in the corresponding period last year. MOL maintains full-year earnings outlook MOL maintained its full-year financial forecast announced on 2 November, projecting consolidated revenue of ¥2.37 trillion and profit attributable to owners of the parent of ¥300 billion for the fiscal year ending 31 March 2027. The company expects its containership business to benefit from continued strong cargo demand and elevated freight rates, although higher fuel costs remain a significant challenge. Its financial outlook assumes that navigation in both the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea will remain unavailable throughout the fiscal year. MOL also expects domestic container terminal volumes to remain under pressure from vessel schedule disruptions, while overseas terminal operations are anticipated to maintain relatively firm handling volumes.
takeaways: Revenue from the segment rose 23.4% to ¥54.3 billion, while MOL recorded ¥64.1 billion in equity-method earnings from ONE, reflecting the carrier’s improved financial performance.
The company said ONE achieved a significant year-on-year improvement in profitability despite higher bunker fuel costs and the suspension of vessel deployments to the Persian Gulf.

articles.title: US Treasury may allow purchase of sanctioned tankers on case basis
articles.summary: The US Treasury Department may allow companies to buy sanctioned shipping vessels and return them to legitimate shipping on a case-by-case basis, according to a government source and a person with knowledge of the matter. “Treasury may consider proposals from legitimate shipping actors to purchase and restore shadow...
articles.body: US Treasury may allow purchase of sanctioned tankers on case basis in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 The US Treasury Department may allow companies to buy sanctioned shipping vessels and return them to legitimate shipping on a case-by-case basis, according to a government source and a person with knowledge of the matter. “Treasury may consider proposals from legitimate shipping actors to purchase and restore shadow fleet vessels to the licit shipping industry on a case-by-case basis,” a US official told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. This approach “ensures that no sanctioned person receives any benefit, and reduces the size of the fleet overall, while helping address pressures on the global energy market,” the US official said. Another source with knowledge of the matter said Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control could be targeting 50-80 sanctioned tankers owned by non-sanctioned companies. There could be 20-30 owners willing to move quickly, the source said. At the end of September, there were a total of 1,225 tankers sanctioned by the US, UK or EU, S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) said in an Oct. 29 shadow tanker report. Of those, 560 were sanctioned by the US. Shadow tankers are increasingly being drawn into the compliant market due to rising freight rates, according to a separate CAS market impact report issued Oct. 23. In 2026, 41 shadow-fleet crude tankers entered compliant trade through Oct. 20, with 68% remaining fully compliant so far, compared with just 17.5% of vessels that remained compliant in 2025. The shift to continued compliance was particularly notable in the third quarter when mainstream tanker earnings surged, the report said. Dirty Arab Gulf-China VLCC freight averaged approximately $197/mt in September, up 77% from August, the report said. CAS defines the shadow fleet as tankers that have transported Iranian or Russian oil in the last two years, vessels subject to US sanctions, and vessels with unknown or suspected false flag registrations. articles.body: Demand Rising in the Ship Recycling Markets in Hellenic Shipping News 12/11/2026 T he ship recycling market has been seeing increased demand for ships. In its latest weekly report, Best Oasis ( www.best-oasis.com ), a leading cash buyer of ships, said that “the Indian ship recycling market remains firm during the week, with buyers showing strong interest in acquiring suitable vessels for recycling. Local steel markets have softened, although the decline in the USD/INR exchange rate has provided some support to buying sentiment. A sanctioned LPG carrier was reportedly sold for recycling into India during the week, with no other sales reported. Overall, market sentiment remains firm, supported by sustained buying interest and continued demand for suitable recycling tonnage. The Bangladeshi ship recycling market continues to remain firm, with buyers actively seeking suitable vessels for recycling. Buying interest remains steady, with prevailing price indications largely unchanged from the previous week. Overall, market sentiment remains positive, supported by firm buying interest and stable pricing levels”. Best Oasis added that “the Pakistani ship recycling market remained largely unchanged this week, with subdued buying interest amid sluggish domestic market conditions. Continued pressure from Iranian imports, including unofficial cross-border trade, has further dampened breakers’ appetite for acquiring vessels. Vessel price indications remain broadly in line with the previous week, while market sentiment continues to range from moderate to subdued, with limited buying activity amid persistent pressure on domestic markets. Finally, the Turkish ship recycling market remains cautious, with limited vessel availability and weak purchasing activity. No new recycling sales were reported during the week, as yards continued to face pressure from weak domestic steel demand, high financing costs and currency depreciation. Buying prices remain relatively uncompetitive compared with India, Bangladesh and Pakistan, limiting Türkiye’s ability to attract conventional recycling tonnage. Nevertheless, Türkiye maintains a competitive position in recycling EU-linked vessels, supported by its proximity to Europe and established environmental compliance standards. Overall, market sentiment remains selective, with limited expectations of a significant recovery in recycling activity in the near term”, the company’s report concluded. articles.body: Tankers In High Demand During October in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 O ctober’s secondhand market showed a clear shift towards tankers, despite little change in overall activity. A total of 168 vessels changed hands, unchanged year on year and 2% above September. Tanker sales rose 61% to 82 vessels, while dry bulk sales fell 30.5% to 57. Tankers accounted for 49% of all transactions, compared with 34% for dry bulk, with their gains offsetting fewer sales elsewhere. Disclosed investment across all sectors reached approximately US$4.7bn, below September’s US$6.6bn. Tankers attracted US$2.9bn, compared with US$1.1bn for dry bulk and US$0.7bn for other vessels. Their share was approximately 62% of total capital, rising to 73% within dry bulk and tankers alone. The stronger tanker weighting therefore accompanied a monthly decline in aggregate spending. Through October, total sales reached 1,481 vessels, up 17% year on year. Dry bulk retained the larger count, with 644 sales against 572 tankers, but tanker purchases grew 68%, compared with 7% for dry bulk. Tankers also attracted US$20.8bn of the US$32.1bn disclosed across these two sectors, versus US$11.3bn for dry bulk. Greek and Chinese buyers followed different patterns. Within dry bulk and tankers, Greek buyers purchased 16 ships in October, evenly split between the sectors; Chinese buyers purchased 12, comprising nine bulkers and three tankers. Over January–October, Greek capital favoured tankers, at US$4.5bn against US$2.1bn in dry bulk. Chinese investment was concentrated in dry bulk, at US$2.5bn versus US$0.6bn in tankers. Chinese capital was also more weighted towards older vessels, while Greek buyers showed a younger dry bulk mix. The overall picture is one of continued investment with the strongest expansion in tanker buying. Dry bulk remains active, but October’s weaker turnover points to a less uniform market. Whether this tanker concentration persists will depend on freight expectations and operating conditions; aggregate spending alone cannot establish rising values for comparable ships. articles.body: Baltic Dry Index Up for 6th Day in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 The Baltic Exchange’s dry bulk freight index, which tracks rates for ships carrying dry bulk commodities, rose by 3.4% to its highest since October 8 at 2,959 points, extending gains for the sixth consecutive session. The capesize index, which typically transports 150,000-ton cargoes, including iron ore and coal, climbed by 5.5% to a peak since October 5 at 4,700 points. Concurrently, the panamax index, which usually carries 60,000 to 70,000 tons of coal or grain, rose by 1.4% to its highest since October 23 at 2,103 points. Among smaller vessels, the supramax index edged up by 0.2% to 1,810 points, halting a 11-session losing run. Source: Baltic Exchange 2026-11-12 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Shipping puts AI readiness to the test with new maturity benchmark in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 L loyd’s Register (LR) has expanded its Digital Maturity Index (DMI) benchmarking tool with a new AI maturity assessment, helping shipowners and operators evaluate their readiness for artificial intelligence as adoption accelerates across the maritime industry. Unveiled at Smart Maritime Network Singapore 2026, the enhanced DMI process introduces AI readiness benchmarking and sector-specific digital use cases while marking a milestone of more than 100 participating organisations. Developed to help maritime organisations benchmark their digital capabilities against industry peers, the DMI enables organisations to assess current capabilities, prioritise investment and accelerate progress towards their digital ambitions. Constantinos Chaelis, Gas Segment Director, LR The new AI maturity assessment examines the foundations required for successful AI adoption, including governance, workforce training, organisational culture, data readiness and performance measurement. It also assesses how AI is being applied across operational areas such as crew management, trade execution, vessel technical management and commercial functions. By looking beyond technology adoption alone, the assessment helps organisations identify whether they have the people, processes and data infrastructure needed to support AI-driven decision making and operational improvement. It also explores industry expectations, perceived opportunities and barriers to implementation. Eleanna Apostolidi, Head of DMI Product Innovation, LR, said: “Across the industry, we’re seeing organisations move beyond AI curiosity and into practical implementation. The challenge is that many companies are investing in AI before fully understanding whether their governance, data and internal capabilities are ready to support it. Eleanna Apostolidi, Head of DMI Product Innovation, LR “The DMI helps organisations establish that baseline. By introducing AI maturity benchmarking, we’re giving shipowners and operators a clearer view of where they are today and what they need to address before they can scale AI with confidence.” Alongside the AI assessment, LR has introduced a range of gas-sector-specific use cases, allowing LNG operators to benchmark the application of digital technologies against operational challenges including boil-off gas management, sloshing risk management, LNG cargo ageing prediction, rollover prevention, pump tripping mitigation, tank maintenance optimisation and brittle fracture monitoring. The additions reflect growing interest in how technologies such as analytics, automation, IoT and digital twins can support safer, more efficient and data-driven LNG operations. Constantinos Chaelis, Gas Segment Director, LR, said: “For LNG operators, digital transformation needs to be grounded in the operational realities of gas shipping. By embedding targeted LNG use cases into the Digital Maturity Index, LR is helping operators benchmark their digital readiness against the specific challenges they face, from cargo management and asset integrity to maintenance planning and operational performance. “The value of the DMI is that it gives the gas sector a structured way to understand where digital capability is already mature, where gaps remain and where investment can be focused to improve safety, efficiency and decision-making across LNG operations.” The DMI helps maritime organisations understand where they are on their digital transformation journey and identify where a clearer roadmap may be needed to turn insight into practical progress. The latest enhancements build on LR’s Digital Transformation Research Programme and support the industry’s transition towards increasingly connected and intelligent operations. articles.body: Global Shipping Report: October U.S. Container Imports Hit Record Volume in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 U.S. containerized imports totaled 2,674,808 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October 2026, up 5.0% from September and 16.0% from October 2025. October marked the highest monthly volume on record, exceeding the previous high set in May 2022 by 2.0%. Through the first 10 months of 2026, imports increased 2.3% from the same period last year. China-origin imports rose for a fourth consecutive month to 987,805 TEUs, the highest monthly volume since January 2025. Imports from the top 10 countries of origin (CoO) increased 5.8% from September, with seven origins posting gains. East and Gulf Coast gateways gained share as Houston, Savannah, Norfolk, and Charleston increased volumes. Gulf Coast imports rebounded 24.0%, while port transit delays increased modestly at seven of the top 10 ports. Trade and routing conditions continue to change. U.S. officials extend the suspension of specified China-related maritime fees, the Panama Canal expanded transit availability, while carriers added Suez-transit services subject to security conditions. Continued Middle East shipping incidents remain a concern for affected trade lanes. For importers, shifting trade conditions reinforce the need to monitor trade policy and port performance, evaluate sourcing and routing alternatives, and maintain flexibility in shipment and inventory planning. U.S. container imports reach a new monthly high in October. U.S. containerized imports increased by 128,547 TEUs (5.0%) from September to 2,674,808 TEUs in October 2026 (see Figure 1). Volume was 16.0% higher than in October 2025 and 29.2% above October 2019. October exceeded the previous high of 2,622,465 TEUs set in May 2022 by 52,343 TEUs (2.0%), making it the largest monthly volume on record. Through October, U.S. container imports were 2.3% higher than in the first 10 months of 2025. October marked the second consecutive month where the year-to-date total exceeded the comparative period in 2025, following eight months where 2026 year-to-date volumes were below last year’s pace. Figure 1: U.S. Container Import Volume Year-over-Year Comparison Source: Descartes Datamyne™ September-to-October volumes increased in nine of the 11 years since 2016 (see Figure 2). October’s 5.0% growth was moderate within that historical pattern and followed declines of 1.0% in 2024 and 0.1% in 2025. The recurring October increase suggests a seasonal pickup, potentially supported this year by extended peak-season demand and uneven cargo arrival timing. October’s record total also built on already elevated September volumes, meaning a moderate monthly increase was sufficient to establish a new high. Figure 2: September to October U.S. Container Import Volume Comparison Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Top 10 U.S. port volumes rise as East and Gulf Coast entries gain. Combined imports across the top 10 U.S. ports increased 4.5% (98,272 TEUs) from September to October 2026 (see Figure 3). Houston posted the largest gain, up 26.7% (42,665 TEUs), followed by Savannah, up 12.6% (30,863 TEUs), Norfolk, up 17.7% (20,557 TEUs), and Charleston, up 18.6% (17,131 TEUs). New York, NY, increased 16.6% (9,081 TEUs), Tacoma 4.8% (3,292 TEUs), and New York/Newark (Newark, NJ) 0.3% (863 TEUs). October’s increases at Savannah, Houston, Norfolk, and Charleston followed declines at all four ports in September. Their combined volume rebounded 18.1% month-over-month but was just 3.6% above August, suggesting the large monthly gains partly reflect recovery from September’s lower volumes. Port data also shows China-origin cargo contributing materially, particularly at Houston and Savannah. Sustained peak-season demand and uneven vessel arrival timing may also have contributed to the rebound. Three West Coast ports declined: Los Angeles fell 1.4% (7,310 TEUs), Long Beach 2.0% (10,156 TEUs), and Oakland 10.9% (8,714 TEUs). The increases at East and Gulf Coast ports more than offset these decreases, indicating that October’s overall growth was uneven across gateways. Figure 3: September to October 2026 Comparison of Import Volumes at Top 10 U.S. Ports Source: Descartes Datamyne™ China-origin imports rise for a fourth consecutive month. U.S. containerized imports from China reached 987,805 TEUs in October 2026, increasing 63,351 TEUs (6.9%) from September and 183,904 TEUs (22.9%) from October 2025 (see Figure 4). October was China’s highest monthly volume since January 2025 and accounted for approximately half of the total U.S. month-over-month increase. China represented 36.9% of total U.S. container imports, up from 36.3% in September. Its October volume remained 3.4% below the July 2024 benchmark of 1,022,913 TEUs. China’s October import mix was led by plastics (HS-39), at 144,530 TEUs (14.6% of China-origin volume), furniture and bedding (HS-94), at 137,551 TEUs (13.9%), and toys, games, and sporting goods (HS-95), at 102,672 TEUs (10.4%). Machinery and electrical machinery (HS-84 and HS-85) accounted for a combined 18.0%, while apparel, made-up textiles, and footwear (HS-61 through HS-64) represented 9.4%. Notable year-over-year gains included plastics, up 30,040 TEUs (26.2%); toys, games, and sporting goods, up 25,185 TEUs (32.5%); articles of iron or steel (HS-73), up 19,240 TEUs (52.1%); and furniture and bedding, up 17,177 TEUs (14.3%). Figure 4: October 2025–October 2026 Comparison of U.S. Total and China-Origin Container Volumes Relative to the July 2024 China-Origin High Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Top 10 countries of origin increase from September. Imports from the top 10 CoO increased by 106,904 TEUs (5.8%) from September to October 2026 (see Figure 5). China led with an increase of 63,351 TEUs (6.9%), followed by South Korea, up 20,871 TEUs (22.8%), and Germany, up 11,808 TEUs (22.8%). Hong Kong added 6,644 TEUs (7.8%), Thailand 4,813 TEUs (4.3%), Indonesia 4,022 TEUs (6.5%), and Japan 1,044 TEUs (1.9%). Germany’s increase partially recovered September’s decrease of 15,212 TEUs. Vietnam fell 3,371 TEUs (1.2%), Taiwan 2,088 TEUs (3.6%), and India 191 TEUs (0.2%). October’s gains were spread across more countries than September’s, when China’s increase largely offset declines elsewhere. Figure 5: September to October 2026 Comparison of U.S. Import Volumes from Top 10 Countries of Origin Source: Descartes Datamyne™ All top 10 countries of origin grow year-over-year. Compared with October 2025, October 2026 imports from the top 10 CoO increased by 304,577 TEUs (18.5%) (see Figure 6). All CoOs posted year-over-year gains: China imports increased 183,904 TEUs (22.9%), approximately 60% of the group’s net gain. South Korea added 22,324 TEUs (24.8%), Vietnam 21,898 TEUs (8.3%), Hong Kong 20,873 TEUs (29.5%), and India 19,540 TEUs (20.4%). Thailand increased 15,801 TEUs (15.6%), Germany 10,594 TEUs (20.0%), Indonesia 4,889 TEUs (8.0%), Taiwan 4,108 TEUs (7.9%), and Japan 647 TEUs (1.2%). Figure 6: October 2025 to October 2026 Comparison of U.S. Import Volumes from Top 10 CoO Source: Descartes Datamyne™ East and Gulf Coast gateways gain share in October. The top five East and Gulf Coast gateways accounted for 39.9% of total U.S. container imports in October 2026, up 3.2 percentage points from the September share of 36.7% (see Figure 7). The top five West Coast gateways accounted for 44.9%, down 2.1 percentage points from 47.0%. Together, the top 10 ports handled 84.8% of U.S. imports, up 1.1 percentage points from September’s 83.7%. Figure 7: September to October 2026 Comparison of U.S. Import Volumes from Top 10 Countries of Origin Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Port transit delays increase modestly at seven of top 10 ports. U.S. container imports have exceeded 2.5 million TEUs in each month since July 2026, while transit delays have increased progressively. The unweighted average across the 10 tracked gateways rose from 4.2 days in June to 4.6 in July, 5.5 in August, 6.0 in September, and 6.3 in October—approximately 50% above June. Nine of the 10 gateways recorded higher delays over that period. October’s modest monthly increase therefore followed several months of accumulating delays, suggesting that sustained high volumes may already be contributing to pressure on the inland logistics network. November’s data will help indicate whether that pressure continues to intensify.Figure 8: Monthly Average Transit Delays (in days) for the Top 10 Ports (August–October 2026) Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Note: Descartes’ definition of port transit delay is the difference, measured in days, between the Estimated Arrival Date initially declared on the bill of lading and the date when Descartes receives the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP)-processed bill of lading data. Changes are calculated before rounding. Gulf Coast imports rebound above their 12-month average. Gulf Coast container imports rose to 266,905 TEUs in October 2026, up 51,582 TEUs (24.0%) from September and 19.7% from October 2025 (see Figure 9). October was 16.2% above the rolling 12-month average of 229,711 TEUs and the highest month since the report began tracking this statistic in August 2023. Houston’s increase of 42,665 TEUs represented approximately 83% of the region’s net monthly gain. However, Houston’s volume had declined 16.5% in September, leaving October imports 5.8% above August and suggesting that the substantial monthly increase partly reflects recovery from September’s lower base. Higher China-origin volumes also contributed to Houston’s rebound. Figure 9: November 2025–October 2026 U.S. Gulf Coast container imports Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Strait of Hormuz incidents sustain regional shipping risk. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) recorded 129 confirmed shipping incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East as of November 5, 2026, including damaged vessels in late October and early November. Continued incidents keep vessel safety, cargo acceptance, and routing under scrutiny. Importers with affected Middle East services should verify current carrier schedules, transit arrangements, and applicable charges, and review alternative routes where available. China-related maritime fee suspension is extended through January 9. The United States Trade Representative (USTR) has finalized a two-month extension of the suspension of its Section 301 action concerning China’s maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors. Effective November 9, 2026, the specified maritime transport service fees and related duties remain suspended through January 9, 2027. USTR will continue reviewing whether a further extension or other action is appropriate. Importers and carriers should monitor developments ahead of the January deadline when reviewing freight-cost assumptions. Panama Canal capacity eases while advance booking remains important. The Panama Canal Authority’s capacity announcement increased daily Neopanamax slots from nine to 10 beginning October 15, bringing combined daily availability across both lock systems to 33 slots. Importers using East and Gulf Coast routings should monitor booking availability and draft limits as carriers plan capacity. Selected Suez services expand while Red Sea risk persists. On November 2, Maersk announced that its India–Europe ME1 Gemini service will now sail via the trans-Suez routing instead of the Cape of Good Hope, with the first westbound departure on November 4 and the first eastbound departure for November 13. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd said service changes remain dependent on regional security conditions. For importers, selective Suez resumptions may shorten transit times on affected services, but continued security risks warrant contingency plans for renewed diversions and potential delivery delays. Los Angeles and Long Beach labor talks continue. The Pacific Maritime Association and watchmen’s union extended their contract through November 20 while mediated negotiations continue. Employers warned that a potential strike could disrupt terminals handling more than half of the two ports’ combined cargo, creating a risk of shipment delays. Managing supply chain risk: what to watch in 2026. In October 2026, U.S. maritime imports reached a record 2.67 million TEUs, up 5.0% month-over-month and 16.0% year-over-year, lifting year-to-date growth to 2.3% compared to the same period in 2025. China’s fourth consecutive monthly increase and gains across seven leading CoOs supported the higher total. East and Gulf Coast gateways gained share, Gulf Coast volume rebounded, and delays increased modestly at most tracked gateways. These conditions warrant monitoring alongside policy decisions and maritime security developments. Here’s what Descartes is monitoring in the months ahead: • Middle East maritime security. Continuing incidents around the Strait of Hormuz can disrupt affected services. Monitor carrier acceptance, routing, and charges as well as security advisories. • Maritime fees and tariff treatment. Track the final decision on the proposed extension of the China-related maritime action suspension and product-level changes affecting landed costs. • Port transit delays. Delays increased at most major gateways in October. Monitor whether these increases persist and build flexibility into delivery schedules and inventory planning to manage potential disruption. • Panama Canal availability. Track reservation access, water conditions, draft limits, and the November slot-allocation competitions as carriers plan early 2027 services. • Red Sea routing. Selected Suez resumptions remain dependent on security. Further diversions could affect vessel deployment, transit times, and schedules. • The economy. The Federal Reserve held its federal funds target range at 3.75%–4.00% on October 28. BEA’s October 29 advance estimate put third-quarter real GDP growth at a 3.4% annualized rate, up from 2.2% in the second quarter. Consumer demand, investment, energy costs, and financing conditions remain relevant to future import demand. Consider recommendations to help minimize global shipping challenges. October’s record volume and uneven port-level changes reinforce the need to assess capacity and sourcing exposure by origin, product, and gateway. Even though overall monthly U.S. imports were elevated, delays and demand conditions are not the same across all trade lanes. Importers should continue to review tariff treatment, regional shipping risks, and carrier routing decisions alongside current trade data. Descartes continues to monitor these developments using Descartes Datamyne™, government releases, and industry intelligence to help organizations identify exposures, assess landed costs, and plan around supply chain disruption. Short-term: • Track port transit delays alongside carrier schedules and local throughput. • Check Middle East and Red Sea advisories for changes to safety, routing, booking acceptance, and applicable charges. • Confirm Panama Canal reservations and current draft limits for affected shipments. • Monitor Los Angeles and Long Beach watchmen negotiations ahead of the November 20 contract deadline and review contingency plans for potentially affected shipments. Near-term: • Assess tariff exposure by HTS code, country of origin, supplier, and entry date; update landed-cost assumptions as treatment changes. • Monitor USTR decisions ahead of the January 9, 2027 suspension expiry and assess potential freight-cost exposure alongside China-origin commodity trends and supplier concentration. • Compare qualified sourcing and routing alternatives using trade volumes, costs, capacity, and delivery requirements. Long-term: • Reevaluate supplier, origin-country, port, and trade-lane concentration to reduce exposure to individual markets and maritime chokepoints. • Maintain flexible sourcing and routing plans that can respond to policy, capacity, delay, and security changes. • Improve landed-cost visibility and scenario planning across multiple suppliers, ports, and transportation options.
