articles.body: Midterms strip out the war premium, but the next two months make shorts a risky bet in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 Crude futures have just posted their sharpest sell-off since 2020. Brent fell 16.6% between the 30 October peak and 4 November. On that day the January contract settled at $94.62/bbl after an $8.98/bbl drop. The trigger was the Democrats’ sweep of both chambers of Congress, which the market read as raising pressure on Washington to wind down the war with Iran. Trend-following CTAs amplified the move, selling around 126 mbbl across crude and products since 30 October, including 52 mbbls on 4 November alone. Brent has since rebounded to around $97/bbl amid fresh tanker incidents in the Hormuz Strait, and prompt spreads have firmed, but it remains on course for a weekly loss of roughly 12%. The sell-off confirms what we flagged in The Crude View and this month’s House View: the war’s price had moved out of the barrel and onto paper, as futures had always been where geopolitical risk premium sits. October was the heaviest month of the war, with 35 vessel attacks. Even so, crude flows exiting the region remained high, averaging 16.6 mbd in October (excluding Iranian oil), down 500 kbd against 17.1 mbd September and also against pre-war flows. Physical weakness has also deepened, as our latest weekly crude report shows. The DFL spread collapsed from as much as +$18/bbl to +$1.70/bbl over the month (Argus) and the North Sea Dated M1-M2 spread fell to -$3.20/bbl on 4 November, its weakest since May 2020. Dubai M1-M2 flipped into contango for the first time since mid-July, and Murban’s premium to Dubai swaps shrank to $4.50/bbl from more than $30/bbl in mid-September (Argus). Aramco cut its December Arab Light OSP to Asia by $2/bbl to a six-year low, below the market at roughly Oman/Dubai -$7/bbl. Freight explains part of this. With PG-China averaging a record $36.60/bbl in October, the freight bill has replaced quality as the thing a differential measures. Sellers inside the Persian Gulf discount to pay it, and grades that cannot pass it on trade at multi-year lows. But freight is not the whole story: Atlantic rates are now falling fast, yet Tupi and Bonny Light arbitrage economics into Asia worsened by around $10/bbl week on week as Dubai’s structure weakened. The underlying driver is supply. Our balances show a 1.1 mbd crude surplus in Q4, the first quarterly surplus this year, as Middle Eastern barrels return. That said, being short futures here is risky. Dated is now trading around $96/bbl, about $9/bbl below our November base case of $105/bbl. The geopolitical risk premium is composed of two layers and prices currently are between the two. First, the risk premium associated with heightened attacks or threats of attacks. Second, the overall distance between the two parties to end the war. The first layer seems to have come out due to the talk of mediation, but the market knows a deal is still needed to resolve the situation. Credible de-escalation headlines could push them lower, but escalation risk is concentrated in the next two months, the window our Compass series laid out in Lame Duck or Angry Duck. Diplomacy is active on the de-escalation path. Trump discussed Qatar’s mediation with its Emir on 6th November, and Washington is reviewing an Iranian nuclear proposal. Doha is also reportedly circulating a two-step plan that would trade the end of the US blockade and some frozen funds for IAEA access and a Hormuz reopening. But Tehran insists Washington must first meet its seven conditions, including sanctions relief, a US withdrawal from the region and reparations. This indicates the two sides are still too far apart. Meanwhile, the more the US waits, the more economic pressure Tehran will feel. Iran has not loaded a crude cargo since 25 August, and we expect its oil revenues (from crude and condensate sales) to hit zero by mid-December. That cliff may raise the risk of further attacks as much as it pushes Tehran towards a deal. On the military side, there are reports that CENTCOM is finalising plans for major combat operations, though no order has been given. The USS Theodore Roosevelt, in Singapore this week, could reach the region from mid-November. Israeli defence officials, for their part, see no major US build-up yet. The outgoing Congress sits until 3 January. After that, Senate leader Chuck Schumer, who has pledged “we will end the war” with some Republican support, will control war powers votes and funding. President Trump will still benefit veto powers, but the window to act militarily will narrow down post-January. Trump’s personality also needs to be accounted for: he could be looking to authorise a strike to later claim victory, or may push further to save his foreign policy legacy. Positioning adds to the asymmetry. Trend CTAs have cut Brent exposure from maximum long to 36% long, meaning a portion of managed money length has gone. However, even in a de-escalation scenario, depleted inventories and US/Chinese restocking should keep a floor near $70/bbl. With physical markets already long but geopolitical risk concentrated before January, heavy short exposure remains highly risky until that window closes. articles.title: Eni, Fincantieri and RINA present the second edition of the Sustainable Maritime Transport Outlook
articles.summary: Eni, a global energy company, Fincantieri, a global leader in the construction of high-complexity ships, and RINA, the global inspection, certification and consulting engineering multinational group, today presented in Rome the second edition of the Sustainable Maritime Transport Outlook, developed with the technical...
articles.body: Eni, Fincantieri and RINA present the second edition of the Sustainable Maritime Transport Outlook in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 Eni, a global energy company, Fincantieri, a global leader in the construction of high-complexity ships, and RINA, the global inspection, certification and consulting engineering multinational group, today presented in Rome the second edition of the Sustainable Maritime Transport Outlook, developed with the technical support of Bain & Company Italy. The Outlook provides a global overview of solutions for decarbonising maritime transport, comparing different technology and fuel options in terms of their emissions reduction potential, maturity, infrastructure availability and the evolution of their Total Cost of Ownership through to 2050. The quantitative analysis is supported by a broad range of interviews with operators and stakeholders across the value chain, including shipowners and operators representing around 40% of the container market and 20% of the cruise market, engine and propulsion technology suppliers accounting for more than 80% of the ICE market, as well as ports and industry associations. Together, these interviews provide a clear picture of market realities. The key message emerging from this second edition is that the landscape is more uncertain than it was a year ago. However, competitive solutions are already available to reduce environmental impact today, offering a pragmatic response to the European regulations currently in force while the industry awaits global decisions from the IMO. Under the Outlook’s reference scenario, “Today as Future”, Europe is expected to achieve an 80% reduction in emissions intensity by 2050 compared with 2020 levels, while the reduction globally is projected at around 40%. The Outlook also considers a slower scenario, “Decarbonization by 2070”, under which the achievement of Europe’s decarbonisation targets is postponed until 2070, with countries in the rest of the world following several years later. Compared with last year, three of the four indicators shaping the transition, namely the regulatory framework, macroeconomic conditions, fuel and infrastructure availability, and technological maturity, have deteriorated, with regulatory uncertainty having the greatest impact. The global IMO agreement has been postponed and, when countries are weighted by tonnage, almost 90% support a more gradual pathway, while the United States has taken a position against maritime decarbonisation. Europe, by contrast, has reaffirmed the targets already established under FuelEU Maritime. The economic outlook has also become more uncertain due to slowing growth, tariffs and geopolitical tensions, while the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz is increasing risks to trade flows and the global economy. The low-emission hydrogen value chain has lost momentum, with numerous maritime projects put on hold. Technology nevertheless continues to play an enabling role, with the orderbook for alternative-fuel vessels growing slowly but steadily. However, against a backdrop of uncertainty, shipowners are increasingly favouring mature, readily available solutions. Synthetic fuels produced from green hydrogen will be essential to complete the pathway to net zero, but they remain expensive and depend on a supply chain that has yet to be fully developed. Through Enilive, Eni is among the leaders in the production of HVO biofuels from renewable feedstocks. These fuels are not only a solution for contributing to decarbonisation, but also an important component of industrial strategy and a means of strengthening the resilience of the production system. Alongside LNG and bio-LNG, biofuels can support maritime transport decarbonisation by leveraging already existing vessels and infrastructure. However, to fully unlock their potential and help the maritime sector progress towards climate neutrality, a regulatory framework is needed that recognises their role across all transport sectors, together with pragmatic and stable operational rules that can support investment development. Fincantieri supports shipowners on their decarbonisation journey through a pragmatic and flexible approach, integrating different technologies and developing innovative solutions. In the cruise sector, LNG is currently the leading alternative fuel, paving the way for progressive decarbonisation through bio-LNG and, in the longer term, e-LNG. Biofuels such as HVO and dual-fuel propulsion systems further broaden the range of available options. At the same time, the Group is working to improve the efficiency of the ship as an integrated system and is developing new energy and propulsion solutions, while also exploring longer-term opportunities through research into nuclear technologies. RINA contributes to the decarbonisation of maritime transport by providing operators across the value chain with its engineering and technological expertise, supporting them in identifying and adopting the most effective solutions. In particular, the Group assesses the technological maturity, practical feasibility and environmental performance of different alternatives, while helping to verify their compliance with regulatory requirements. The Outlook therefore sets out concrete commitments for every player across the value chain: common rules and standards for regulators and certification bodies; targeted investment and flexible infrastructure for ports; availability and diversification for fuel suppliers; vessels designed to accommodate multiple solutions and retrofit support for shipyards and shipowners; and continued investment in research and development by engine manufacturers. Pragmatism does not mean waiting: it means starting with mature technologies while building platforms that can evolve over time. Against the backdrop of an increasingly complex geopolitical environment, Eni, Fincantieri and RINA also formalised their commitment during the event to continue the Observatory’s work for the next three years. The signing of the agreement marks the first step in a collaborative journey that is expected to deepen and become increasingly strategic, with the potential to involve additional players across the value chain in the future. The cost landscape changes over time in Europe, where progressive decarbonisation targets are underpinned by a system of increasing penalties. In 2030, fossil fuels remain the most cost-effective options, while synthetic fuels can cost around three times as much. From 2040 onwards, European emissions penalties make biofuels increasingly competitive, and by 2050 fossil fuels could cost around twice as much as the more sustainable alternatives. Looking at Europe’s fuel mix in 2050, there is no single clear winner, but a well-defined backbone emerges: biofuels will account for around one third of the mix, alongside fossil and bio-LNG, while synthetic fuels will contribute around 20% to the decarbonisation pathway. Overall, this will result in an 80% reduction in GHG emissions compared with 2020 levels. Compared with the previous edition, the overall direction of the transition remains unchanged, but the projected contribution of synthetic fuels has been reduced by around half. As a result, the investment required to upgrade European port infrastructure is also lower: approximately $15 billion, compared with the roughly $25 billion estimated last year, with the entire difference attributable to the slower uptake of synthetic fuels. At global level, the transition is expected to progress more slowly. By 2050, the global fuel mix will still rely significantly on conventional fuels, which will account for around 70% of the total, while GHG emissions reductions will reach only around 40% compared with 2020 levels. In Europe, by contrast, biofuels and LNG will remain the main areas of convergence with the rest of the world, albeit within a faster emissions reduction pathway. In the cruise sector, which is of strategic importance to the Italian shipbuilding industry, synthetic fuels are expected to play a greater role than in maritime transport overall. This will primarily involve e-LNG, which could help decarbonise LNG-powered vessels already in the fleet while making the most of investments already made in existing platforms. Although nuclear propulsion is not expected to make a significant contribution to the 2050 decarbonisation pathway, the first nuclear-powered vessels could enter service between 2040 and 2045. Over the longer term, nuclear could also emerge as a key technology for certain high-power, long-range segments. This makes it important to begin research, assessment and development activities in this field today. Finally, the decarbonisation of maritime transport will require coordinated action across the entire value chain. Stakeholder interviews highlight a number of common barriers: regulatory uncertainty, which is holding back investment; the difficulty of passing the additional cost of lower-emission fuels on to customers; and bottlenecks that are more pronounced onshore than onboard vessels. Accelerating the transition will require a more stable global framework, consistent price signals, sufficiently predictable demand, reliable fuel volumes and greater feedstock diversification. articles.title: Freightos Weekly Update: LA/LB strike deadline extended; Dem win increasing trade uncertainty
articles.summary: Last week’s US midterm election results saw Republicans lose control of both houses of Congress, raising questions about possible implications for trade and logistics. On the one hand, the shift, reflecting voter concerns over inflation including from tariffs and energy prices, could mean the White House will seek to...
articles.body: Last week’s US midterm election results saw Republicans lose control of both houses of Congress, raising questions about possible implications for trade and logistics. On the one hand, the shift, reflecting voter concerns over inflation including from tariffs and energy prices, could mean the White House will seek to avoid introducing new tariffs and aim to deescalate the war in Iran in the hopes of bringing oil prices down. On the other hand, with President Trump likely to face difficulties passing new legislation, the election may embolden the president to focus and act on foreign and trade policy which is less easily influenced by Congress. In recent months the administration has trended toward deescalation in trade relations with China. And post the election late last week, both sides officially extended the pause on reciprocal port call fees until January 10th, aligning with the extension of the other elements of the interim US-China agreement announced back in September. Presidents Trump and Xi will meet in China next week. This year’s many trade war twists and turns may have helped drive the unusually early and then unusually long transpacific ocean peak season that has kept US container import volumes elevated since May. A lower effective tariff regime on many US trading partners including China following the Supreme Court’s IEEPA invalidation in February, and anticipation that duties would increase in July may have spurred some of the frontloading that started in May. But tariffs that stayed about level in July and beyond, IEEPA refunds that infused many importers with unexpected cash, and surprisingly resilient consumer spending may all have helped keep the rally going. The latest National Retail Federation US ocean import volume report shows container arrivals started climbing in May but continued their ascent through the summer peaking at just below record levels in September at 2.37 million TEU. Volumes are estimated to have eased 5% in October with November volumes projected to be down 14% from the September high. The report estimates that year totals will be 2.2% stronger than in 2025, following earlier expectations of flat volumes or even more modest growth. Slowing demand may be one factor in transpacific container rates easing slightly last week as significant carrier GRIs failed to materialize. But at $8,200/FEU to the West Coast and $9,700/FEU to the East Coast, prices are still at about peak levels. The ILWU Local 26 watchmen union has extended its strike deadline to November 20th to allow more time for negotiations with operators at the ports of LA and Long Beach with the aim of averting a potentially disruptive walk out. Though most holiday season merchandise has by now already arrived at the ports, a lot of goods still need to be moved inland, with a serious rail backlog slowing progress for many importers and making the prospect of a strike even more concerning. Carriers seem to have abandoned November 1st GRI hopes for Asia – Europe lanes as well, as prices dipped 5% last week to $3,400/FEU to North Europe and 1% to $4,300/FEU to the Mediterranean. Though rates aren’t climbing for now, prices are well above last year’s levels with N. Europe rates up 50% year on year and Mediterranean prices up 88%. Air rates out of the Far East continued to climb last week on peak season demand. China – US prices increased 3% to more than $8.00/kg, already reaching last year’s high that was hit only in mid-December 2025. China – Europe rates increased 11% to $4.87/kg, and are up 23% year on year. Part of the rate strength is due to a higher floor, propped up by still-elevated jet fuel prices. For some lanes, especially many Far East – N. America routes, strong demand from data center hardware volumes has kept pressure on rates and also helped set the high starting point for peak season spot prices. Some observers speculate however that Democrat control over Congress could mean tighter AI regulations that could slow data center hardware volume growth to the US. Transatlantic air cargo rates have climbed by 33% over the last month to $2.90/kg as capacity reductions from winter schedules – as well as possible freighter shifts to higher volume lanes – and peak season demand combine to put pressure on rates. Best, Judah Levine, Head of Research Freightos Group (Nasdaq: CRGO)

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Garry2014 / Shutterstock (Bloomberg) — A tanker carrying Russian diesel that had briefly signaled the US made a U-turn about 400 nautical miles off New York, compounding uncertainty over deliveries to the North American market. The Agioi Fanendes , hauling about 40,000 metric tons of ultralow-sulfur diesel, or almost 300,000 barrels, started to move away from the US East Coast and has been dawdling in a zigzag pattern since Monday, according to a port report and ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Traders are closely watching movements of Russian diesel after President Vladimir Putin agreed to supply fuel to the US and global markets in a deal with President Donald Trump last month. The arrangement sparked criticism from US Democrats, who argued it would help the Kremlin finance its war in Ukraine, and so far no Russian diesel cargo has reached America, tracking data show. The Agioi Fanendes signaled New York after departing Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk in late October and later switched its destination to “for orders.” The tanker is still “proceeding for orders as the discharging port is not confirmed yet,” vessel manager Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Ltd. said in an email, repeating a previous response to a question about the ship’s movement. Russia said last month it had loaded four tankers with diesel destined for the US, in line with the Putin-Trump agreement, according to Interfax. The deal was aimed at lowering fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, though Democrats argued it would be too limited to do so. There’s also some doubt over whether Russia would be able to export as much diesel as it promised amid Ukraine’s renewed bombardment of the country’s refineries. Since the start of November, six Russian refineries have come under attack, according to a Bloomberg tally based on statements from people familiar with the incidents. That equates to total design capacity of around 1.7 million barrels a day, Bloomberg calculations show. In late October, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the country aimed to export more than 2 million tons of diesel to global markets in November. But he added that Ukrainian attacks may trim available supplies. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: U.S. Ethanol Could Fuel Growing Fleet of Methanol-Capable Ships, Study Finds
articles.summary: A new study says the United States has enough spare ethanol production capacity to supply a meaningful share of the global marine fuel market, offering shipowners another fuel option as...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Tangier Maersk at the Port of Mobile. Photo credit: Alabama Port Authority. A new study says the United States has enough spare ethanol production capacity to supply a meaningful share of the global marine fuel market, offering shipowners another fuel option as the number of methanol-capable vessels continues to grow. The report, Marine Ethanol: Unlocking the US Opportunity , published Wednesday by the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance (MEMA), argues that ethanol could be used in existing methanol dual-fuel engines and bunkering infrastructure with relatively minor modifications, potentially easing concerns over the availability of low-emission methanol. According to the study, more than 300 methanol-capable vessels are already operating or on order, creating a potential market for ethanol either as a standalone marine fuel or blended with methanol. The United States is particularly well-positioned to meet that demand. U.S. ethanol plants have an annual production capacity of approximately 18.5 billion gallons, compared with actual production of 16.4 billion gallons in 2025, leaving roughly 2 billion gallons of unused capacity. The country already accounts for slightly more than half of global fuel ethanol production and exports to approximately 80 countries, supported by an established distribution network that includes Gulf Coast terminals near major bunkering hubs. The study estimates that supplying just 1% of shipping’s annual fuel consumption by mass would require approximately 1 billion gallons of ethanol, an amount that could be covered by existing U.S. spare capacity. A 5% market share by the mid-2030s would require around 5 billion gallons annually, necessitating additional production or a shift in existing demand. The findings come as ethanol begins moving beyond demonstration projects and into commercial shipping operations. In September, A.P. Moller-Maersk completed the first publicly announced commercial ship-to-ship ethanol bunkering of a deep-sea containership in the United States. The operation involved the dual-fuel Tangier Maersk , which received U.S.-produced corn ethanol in Houston. As gCaptain reported at the time, the operation was intended to provide practical experience with ethanol sourcing, handling, bunkering and onboard use as Maersk explores additional fuel options for its growing fleet of alcohol-capable vessels. Engine developer WinGD subsequently confirmed that the vessel successfully sailed from Houston to New York using ethanol, marking the first in-service operation of its X-DF-M/E alcohol-fuel engine platform on the fuel. The new study rates ethanol’s technology readiness at level 8–9, indicating that the underlying technology is mature, although widespread commercial deployment remains at an early stage. It also highlights ethanol’s potential to reduce conventional air pollutants compared with heavy fuel oil. According to the report, ethanol virtually eliminates sulfur oxide emissions, reduces nitrogen oxides by 40% to 94%, depending on engine technology, and cuts particulate matter by 90% to 99%. Those reductions concern emissions from fuel combustion rather than ethanol’s overall lifecycle greenhouse gas footprint, which depends on feedstock, production methods and supply-chain emissions. The study also identifies potential cost advantages. It estimates ethanol’s net production cost, after accounting for revenue from co-products, at less than $1 per gallon, although that figure does not represent the delivered price of marine fuel. Despite those advantages, significant hurdles remain before ethanol can become a widely traded marine fuel. These include developing consistent fuel specifications, establishing reliable certification and traceability systems, and ensuring that ethanol can meet the environmental requirements of emerging shipping regulations. “Ethanol is moving beyond pilots, and this study shows the United States has the production base and export infrastructure to supply shipping at scale,” said Clarence Woo, managing director of the Global Centre for Green Fuels. “The next challenge is consistency. As international bunkering grows, shipping needs standardised and fungible marine fuel specifications, together with traceable feedstocks and a robust chain of custody, so that ethanol from different producers and regions can be used with confidence.” The study arrives as the International Maritime Organization prepares for another round of negotiations over its proposed Net-Zero Framework. The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee is scheduled to meet from November 30 to December 3, with a resumed extraordinary session provisionally planned for December 4, subject to confirmation. The discussions could influence how alternative fuels are assessed and rewarded under future international shipping emissions rules. For U.S. ethanol producers, the marine fuel market represents a potential new source of demand, while shipowners could gain access to an established fuel supply chain without waiting for production of renewable methanol to expand. However, the study’s projections remain illustrative, and the extent to which ethanol can compete with other marine fuels will depend on its delivered cost, lifecycle carbon intensity, regulatory treatment and commercial acceptance. The report was published by MEMA, a platform of the Singapore-based Global Centre for Green Fuels. Classification society ABS provided technical analysis as a knowledge partner, while U.S. ethanol producer Marquis Energy contributed industry input. The findings and recommendations are those of MEMA. articles.title: Russian Diesel Faces U.S. Buyer Resistance Despite Trump Sanctions Waiver
articles.summary: US companies are unlikely to import Russian diesel as a tanker full of the fuel idles off the US Eastern Seaboard, experts said, despite President Donald Trump's temporary waiver of some sanctions on Moscow's fuel exports.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Shutterstock/bob63 By Arathy Somasekhar, Lisa Baertlein and Nicole Jao HOUSTON, Nov 11 (Reuters) – US companies are unlikely to import Russian diesel as a tanker full of the fuel idles off the US Eastern Seaboard, experts said, despite President Donald Trump’s temporary waiver of some sanctions on Moscow’s fuel exports. Banks are likely to be reluctant to finance US deals for Russian diesel, the experts said, noting there are legal questions about whether the president’s waiver is enough to allow for the imports. There are also operational challenges, because importers would need to blend the Russian diesel to meet US heating oil specifications. US lawmakers from both parties objected last month, when Trump temporarily waived parts of a law that slapped Moscow with sanctions after its invasion of Ukraine. Former President Joe Biden imposed the sanctions after the 2022 invasion, and Congress later backed them and codified them as law. Looking to lower diesel prices that spiked during the US-Israeli war on Iran, Trump’s plan would allow Russia to immediately export 300,000 tons, or 2.25 million barrels, of diesel to US and global markets. This would be followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” The price of diesel in the US was $6.13 per gallon on Wednesday, according to the American Automobile Association. That is down 20 cents a gallon from $6.33 the day that Trump waived the sanctions in October but up 63% from $3.76 before the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February, according to AAA data. A tanker carrying the first cargo of Russian diesel for the US halted its voyage off the East Coast this week, shipping data showed on Tuesday. Its operator said the destination had not yet been decided. On Tuesday, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he was confident the idled tanker would help supply global markets even if it did not land at a US port. “We just want that diesel going into the world markets,” Wright told reporters at an event in New Orleans. Last month, the US Treasury Department issued a general license temporarily permitting imports of Russian diesel. But any buyers could damage their reputation and also face legal risks if they engage in such “prohibited but authorized transactions,” said Jeremy Paner, a partner at law firm Hughes Hubbard & Reed and a former US sanctions official. Paner said any savings from buying cheaper Russian diesel could easily be wiped out by the need to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees from likely upcoming congressional investigations. “It’s a relatively easy call for businesses to say, ‘We don’t want to touch it,’” Paner said. POLITICAL BLOWBACK Dozens of US senators, including six Republicans, have called on Trump to rescind ?the deal, saying it helps Russia fund attacks on Ukraine and has no benefit to Americans. New Jersey’s Democratic Governor Mikie Sherrill has warned local port officials and terminal operators against accepting Russian diesel, saying those shipments would break federal law. A handful of laws prohibit importing Russian oil products, analysts and lawyers said. Several jurisdictions, including the UK and the EU, also sanction Russian crude and fuel. US Representative Jamie Raskin of the House Judiciary Committee said in a letter that importers would remain liable “long after the current administration leaves office.” The letter to oil industry groups and the US Chamber of Commerce cited a 10-year statute of limitations. “Your members are now on notice that taking part in any effort to help President (Vladimir) Putin hawk Russian diesel in the US is a clear and dangerous violation of federal law,” he wrote. A Trump administration official said the temporary waiver was in compliance with all applicable laws. Still, finding a willing US importer might prove difficult. Banks are unlikely to finance deals related to a Russian diesel trade, which could violate sanctions in other countries, said David Tannenbaum, director of sanctions consultancy Blackstone Compliance Services and a former US Treasury sanctions specialist. “The money that’s on the table for a single deal in comparison to the compliance costs and potential headaches, I would be a hard pass,” he said, adding that every party downstream that touches the cargo and distributes it was a potential subject for an investigation in the US Congress. The Russian diesel would also need to be blended to meet New York Mercantile Exchange heating oil specifications, adding another deterrent for importers, Natalia Losada, an analyst at Energy Aspects, wrote in a note, adding that cargoes may still end up diverting to Brazil or other more traditional destinations for Russian diesel. “If the first vessel is unable to dock or discharge in any US ports, that does create that bit of a hurdle for every further vessel that is on its way,” said Janiv Shah, a vice president at consultancy Rystad Energy. articles.title: OPEC+ Oil Production Rises in October, Nearing Pre-Iran War Rates
articles.summary: OPEC+ crude oil production jumped in October, led by a sharp increase in output from Saudi Arabia despite continued disruption to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the Iran war.The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization…
articles.body: OPEC+ Oil Production Rises in October, Nearing Pre-Iran War Rates Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 11, 2026 © CURIOS - stock.adobe.com OPEC+ crude oil production jumped in October, led by a sharp increase in output from Saudi Arabia despite continued disruption to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the Iran war. The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23 million barrels per day in October, OPEC said in a monthly report on Wednesday, up about 2.04 million bpd from September. The figures, based on secondary sources, add to signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports by using workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers to bypass disruption caused by the conflict. According to Reuters calculations based on OPEC data, October output was equivalent to 97% of the 42.72 million bpd produced by OPEC+ in February. Saudi Arabia told OPEC it pumped 10.563 million bpd in October, the report said, up from 8.372 million bpd in September. That was its highest output since February, when it reported production of 10.882 million bpd. Riyadh sharply increased its production in February ahead of US and Israeli strikes on Iran. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez has called on governments to step up enforcement of international maritime regulations in the Strait of Hormuz, warning that unsafe shipping practices are adding to the risks facing seafarers amid the ongoing conflict. In a statement issued Wednesday, Dominguez raised concerns about vessels transiting the strategic waterway without complying with basic international safety requirements, including provisions of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS). The warning comes as commercial shipping continues to face attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz, where the IMO has now verified more than 130 incidents involving merchant vessels since the conflict began on February 28. At least 25 seafarers have been killed, while others remain missing or have been injured. “IMO’s technical and operational regulations are there to protect seafarers, ships and the marine environment. They must be respected and enforced effectively,” Dominguez said. The IMO chief specifically cited reports of substandard vessels, ships concealing their IMO identification numbers, vessels operating under fraudulent registrations or false flags, and other unsafe practices. The concerns add another dimension to the shipping crisis in the Persian Gulf, where vessels already face significant security risks from ongoing hostilities. Dominguez’s comments highlight the need for governments to enforce existing maritime regulations even as the conflict complicates commercial navigation. He called on flag states, port states and coastal states to take action against violations within their respective jurisdictions and in accordance with international law. “I strongly urge shipowners and operators to refrain from commercial activities in the Strait that expose seafarers to unacceptable risks,” Dominguez said. The latest appeal follows last week’s meeting of the IMO Council in London, where member states called for stronger protections for seafarers and reiterated that vital shipping lanes must remain open, safe and secure. During the November 2–6 meeting, the Council condemned attacks on merchant shipping and called on governments to refrain from unlawful measures that endanger seafarers and international navigation. According to the IMO’s latest incident records, 133 incidents had been confirmed as of November 10, with 25 seafarer fatalities. Dominguez also renewed his call for a political solution to the crisis, urging governments to restore a safe, internationally recognized framework for navigation through the Strait of Hormuz that preserves established rights and freedoms of navigation. He warned that the conflict’s consequences extend well beyond the maritime industry, contributing to higher living costs for millions of people worldwide. “It is imperative for Governments to tackle the root causes of this conflict,” he said. articles.summary: The Panama Canal is increasing its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and restoring the maximum allowable draft at its Neopanamax locks to 50 feet, easing restrictions as improved water...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Panama Canal Authority The Panama Canal is increasing its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and restoring the maximum allowable draft at its Neopanamax locks to 50 feet, easing restrictions as improved water conditions provide some relief from concerns over another prolonged El Niño. The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) announced the changes in a November 9 advisory to shipping, citing improving lake levels, favorable hydrological forecasts and the effectiveness of water-saving measures implemented at the locks. The adjustment adds one daily booking slot for Super vessels at the Panamax locks, increasing availability in that category from 18 to 19. Total daily reservation capacity rises from 33 to 34 slots, including 24 at the Panamax locks and 10 at the larger Neopanamax locks. The ACP also raised the maximum authorized draft for Neopanamax vessels to 15.24 meters (50 feet), effective immediately and until further notice. The increase follows an October adjustment that raised the allowable draft to 49 feet. The latest changes mark another shift in the canal’s operating outlook after months of concern over deteriorating water conditions and the potential for a prolonged El Niño event. As gCaptain reported in September, canal officials had postponed a planned reduction in the Neopanamax draft limit to 47.5 feet after reassessing Gatun Lake levels and rainfall projections. At the time, the canal was maintaining a 48-foot draft limit while warning that below-normal precipitation could persist for months. The concerns followed the historic 2023–2024 drought , which forced the canal to sharply restrict vessel transits and drafts, disrupting global shipping schedules and sending some cargoes on longer routes. At the worst point of that drought, daily transit capacity fell to just 22 vessels. The waterway has faced additional pressure this year as disruptions in the Middle East have redirected shipping traffic toward Panama, increasing competition for available transit reservations, particularly among energy carriers. The additional Panamax booking slot will be introduced in stages. For transit dates November 12–17, it will be available through the canal’s auction system. For November 18–23, it will be offered through the Special Competition booking period. Beginning with November 24 transit dates, the slot will become available through the regular Second Competition Period. Despite the improved outlook, the ACP continues to emphasize the importance of advance reservations. Its Transit Reservation System remains the only way to guarantee a transit date, and vessels arriving without bookings could face substantial delays. The authority said it will continue monitoring rainfall, watershed conditions and lake levels, with further operational adjustments possible as conditions change. The latest increase offers shipping companies greater flexibility heading into the final weeks of 2026, although the canal’s ability to sustain the higher capacity will continue to depend on freshwater availability. articles.summary: The UK is moving ahead with a £90 million investment in autonomous underwater systems, advanced sensors and artificial intelligence to strengthen the Royal Navy’s ability to track Russian submarines and...

Join the leading maritime news network Illustration courtesy Ocean Infinity The UK is moving ahead with a £90 million investment in autonomous underwater systems, advanced sensors and artificial intelligence to strengthen the Royal Navy’s ability to track Russian submarines and protect critical infrastructure in the North Atlantic. The initiative, known as Atlantic Net, is the first operational phase of the Royal Navy’s broader Atlantic Bastion programme, which aims to combine crewed warships and submarines with autonomous systems to improve underwater surveillance and counter potential threats to subsea communications cables, energy networks and shipping routes. The UK Ministry of Defence announced the investment Tuesday during the International Sea Power Conference in Oslo, Norway, alongside a framework agreement with UK-based marine robotics company Ocean Infinity Solutions. GOV.UK Under the arrangement, Ocean Infinity will serve as the Royal Navy’s commercial mission partner, helping develop and operate a network of autonomous and remotely operated systems capable of maintaining persistent surveillance across the North Atlantic. The system will combine underwater sensors, uncrewed platforms, communications technology and AI-powered data analysis to detect and track potentially hostile submarine activity. The information will provide Royal Navy warships and Astute-class attack submarines with earlier warnings and a clearer picture of threats beneath the surface. The programme is expected to become operational in 2027, according to UK Defence Minister Luke Pollard, who outlined the plans in a speech in Oslo. “The threats beneath the North Atlantic are changing, and we are changing with them,” Pollard said. “This investment gives the Royal Navy new technology to find threats earlier and protect our critical infrastructure, while also backing British business.” The investment comes amid growing concern among European governments and NATO allies over the vulnerability of underwater infrastructure, particularly communications cables and energy connections that are essential to both civilian economies and military operations. Atlantic Bastion is intended to expand the Navy’s ability to monitor these networks while strengthening anti-submarine warfare capabilities and supporting the protection of Britain’s nuclear deterrent. For Ocean Infinity, the agreement marks a significant expansion of its role in defense and maritime security. The company, which has developed autonomous and remotely operated marine systems for commercial operations, said Atlantic Net represents a shift toward sustained underwater surveillance using a combination of uncrewed, autonomous and smaller-crewed platforms. “The Royal Navy has been exploring how to move beyond traditional, heavily crewed fleets towards a broader mix of robotic and lean-crewed platforms,” said Joe Robinson, President of Solutions at Ocean Infinity. “Atlantic Net is that idea coming to life.” Ocean Infinity said its role will include integrating maritime platforms, underwater sensors, communications, remote operations and data services into a coordinated surveillance capability directed by the Royal Navy. Ocean Infinity The £90 million framework is also expected to support nearly 200 skilled jobs within Ocean Infinity and its immediate supply chain, according to the Ministry of Defence. The programme will operate alongside NATO and Joint Expeditionary Force allies, with the goal of expanding the scale and persistence of underwater surveillance across the North Atlantic. The announcement also forms part of a broader British push toward a hybrid naval fleet that uses autonomous technology to supplement traditional warships and submarines, allowing the Royal Navy to monitor larger areas without relying entirely on crewed vessels. REUTERS/Hannibal Hanschke//File Photo By Holger Hansen BERLIN, Nov 11 (Reuters) – The German government will go ahead with a planned 24-terawatt-hour crisis gas reserve to be funded by user surcharges, the economy ministry said, following criticism over missed storage targets for the winter heating season this year. The state buffer, which amounts to about 10% of the nation’s gas storage capacity, will be accumulated over up to three years, the ministry said in a statement on Wednesday. It said the move would address severe disruptions, for example from acts of sabotage, and does not replace the private sector’s seasonal stock-keeping duties. “The gas reserve does not relieve market participants of their responsibilities, which include winter preparedness as well as meeting supply obligations,” it said. To fund the reserve, households would likely face 0.3% to 0.5% higher gas prices, the ministry said. Opposition parties and Italy have criticized Germany’s low gas storage levels , which stood at 62% at end-October, below a target of 70%. Berlin has said its supplies are still secure as it now has more purchasing options via liquefied natural gas terminals and through pipelines from Norway than it had in 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine triggered an energy crisis. The government also plans a range of measures to tighten gas market regulation, including mandatory seasonal stock keeping for gas utilities, a ministry spokesperson told Reuters on Wednesday. A person close to the matter said the plans include closer monitoring of inventories by the network regulator, while the government is also considering measures to secure gas supplies to power plants and industrial sites. Documents seen by Reuters showed that setting up the reserve will likely cost between €1.26 billion ($1.41 billion) and €1.81 billion, plus running costs. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo By Ruth Liao and Stephen Stapczynski Nov 11, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Polish energy company Orlen SA terminated one of its long-term liquefied natural gas contracts with QatarEnergy, citing the export giant’s inability to deliver as the conflict in the Middle East disrupts shipments. The annulment is the first by a customer of QatarEnergy, which supplied about a fifth of the world’s LNG until the war between the US and Iran throttled its shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged its export infrastructure. It is another blow for the emirate, as the nation’s budget deficit increases because of the lost revenue. Missile strikes in March damaged the world’s largest LNG export plant in Qatar — badly damaging two of its 14 production units and forcing the supplier to declare force majeure, a legal clause allowing producers to miss deliveries due to factors beyond their control, on shipments for the first time. Iranian attacks on vessels continue to slow shipping through Hormuz, cutting gas flows to a third of pre-war levels last month. The inability to meet contractual obligations led to the dissolving of the contract that was meant to run until 2034 and had an estimated value of €570 million ($637 million) this year, Orlen said in a statement on Tuesday. The agreement remains in force for a further 60 days. Orlen will retain a second supply contract with Qatar. Qatar sells most of its fuel under long-term contracts and has put its customers in Europe and Asia on force majeure notice for months. That’s forced buyers to replace the supply with spot cargoes, prices for which are at the highest level in years. Extended use of the clause eventually gives buyers the right to walk away, typically after a prolonged period of canceled deliveries. Qatar has been extending the measure every month, with its latest notice affecting shipments through the end of the year. Buyers are “unable to make longer term arrangements for alternative supply if their Qatari contract remains on foot, because if the volumes return at some point, it would leave the customer with an overly contracted position,” said Saul Kavonic, senior energy analyst at MST Marquee. “The longer the disruption lasts, the more customers will come under pressure to pursue this alternative.” Read More: Qatar Rewrites Its Gas Playbook With Old Tankers and New Tactics The canceled Qatari contract was Poland’s first LNG purchase agreement, paving the way for the European country to begin importing the super-chilled fuel in 2015. The contract was priced at 16% of Brent oil, according to a BloombergNEF database of LNG contracts, making it among the most expensive term deals in effect. Orlen’s second deal with Qatar is linked to natural gas benchmarks. Meanwhile, the Polish company has signed deals to procure LNG from projects in Texas and Louisiana including Port Arthur and Plaquemines — more affordable and flexible options that allows its trading desk to resell shipments. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: Tanker Operator Furetank Nabs International Award Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 11, 2026 Image courtesy Furetank Swedish tanker operator Furetank has been named a regional winner of the EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2026 awards, receiving the Best International Growth distinction for combining fleet expansion, technological innovation and environmental performance. The award recognizes Furetank's long-term investment strategy, which has helped position the company as a leader in developing more environmentally efficient product tankers while maintaining profitable growth. Lars Höglund, who has led the company's development for nearly four decades, accepted the award during a ceremony at Hotel Elite Park Avenue in Gothenburg. The jury highlighted Höglund's commitment to technological innovation, employee involvement and sustainable development in one of the world's most capital-intensive industries. "For almost four decades, this entrepreneur has made bold, long-term investments in one of the world's riskiest and most capital-intensive industries," the jury stated, recognizing Furetank's emphasis on safety, workplace culture and continuous improvement. Furetank's growth has been closely tied to its VINGA vessel series, developed in cooperation with FKAB Marine Design. The company and its partners have ordered 26 tankers in the series, designed to reduce the environmental footprint of petroleum product transportation. The business has grown from a family operation with a single tanker in the 1950s to a shipping company employing approximately 300 people and generating annual revenue of SEK 1.5 billion. "It all goes back to a point ten years ago when we had to renew our fleet, just as society was turning its attention to the environment," Höglund said. "Together with FKAB Marine Design, we developed a vessel design that today gives us the ships with the smallest environmental footprint in their class globally." Höglund said the fleet investment demonstrated that improved environmental performance and commercial profitability can go hand in hand. Furetank will advance to the Swedish national EY Entrepreneur Of The Year final, scheduled for January 27, 2027, at Stockholm City Hall. Image courtesy Furetank

articles.body: Balaena, Kongsberg Team Up to Bring Arctic Hunter USV to Royal Navy Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 11, 2026 (Credit: Baleana) British shipbuilding group Balaena and Norway's Kongsberg Maritime have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to advance the Arctic Hunter uncrewed surface vessel (USV), a proposed solution for the Royal Navy's emerging Type 92 anti-submarine warfare requirement. The agreement, signed at Kongsberg Maritime's offices in Norway on November 11, builds on an existing relationship between the companies and aims to combine British shipbuilding capabilities with Norwegian vessel design and autonomous technologies. Arctic Hunter is designed for uncrewed naval operations in extreme Arctic conditions, combining Kongsberg Maritime's commercial vessel designs and remote and autonomous technologies with sonar and military communications capabilities from UK defence technology company Thales. The proposed vessel is intended to provide persistent submarine detection capabilities in the High North, using a commercial shipbuilding approach designed to accelerate construction and delivery. Under the proposed program, the vessels would be built at Balaena's Birkenhead shipyard in the UK, with the ambition of delivering units ready for military integration before the end of the decade. The Birkenhead facility has four large dry docks, a non-tidal wet basin, fabrication facilities and a dedicated modular construction hall. Headquartered in Cornwall, Balaena employs more than 2,000 people and operates shipbuilding, repair and engineering facilities across the UK and Gibraltar, including 12 dry docks. The companies intend to use their collaboration to support the development of future naval capabilities and strengthen maritime security across the North Atlantic and High North.

articles.body: Physical AI in Shipbuilding: Fincantieri Partners with Poste Italiane, TIM Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 11, 2026 Copyright Casimiro/AdobeStock New industrial AI initiative targets shipyard automation, robotics and preservation of technical expertise across Fincantieri's global shipbuilding operations. Italian shipbuilding group Fincantieri has announced a strategic partnership with Poste Italiane and telecommunications company TIM to establish Italy's first integrated national Physical AI ecosystem, designed to accelerate the application of artificial intelligence, robotics and automation in shipbuilding. The initiative, called "Fincantieri Ontology," is a central component of the company's 2026–2030 industrial plan, F4 (Fast Forward Further Future), which prioritizes digitalization, automation and the protection of industrial knowledge. The partnership combines the three companies' technological capabilities to develop a secure digital infrastructure that integrates AI directly into ship design, construction and vessel management. Fincantieri Ontology will focus on automating shipyard design and production processes, while the parallel "Navis Sapiens" initiative targets the digitalization of ships themselves, ultimately supporting increasingly autonomous vessel operations. A key element involves creating digital representations of industrial processes, capturing technical expertise and using AI models to optimize manufacturing operations. The companies plan to develop four-dimensional design and construction models, enabling shipyard workers and robotic systems to receive AI-optimized work packages and daily production instructions. The initiative supports Fincantieri's industrial workload valued at approximately $81 billion (€70 billion), extending through 2036. Its supply chain includes 7,000 small and medium-sized enterprises, 18 shipyards worldwide and approximately 100,000 people accessing its facilities daily. Another objective is preserving accumulated shipbuilding knowledge while transitioning traditional manufacturing roles toward digitally enabled production. "Data and Artificial Intelligence are the driving forces behind our 2026–2030 Industrial Plan," said Pierroberto Folgiero, CEO and General Manager of Fincantieri. "With the launch of this strategic partnership, we are not simply digitalizing an industrial process; we are documenting and protecting the ontology of our technical culture." Fincantieri said the partnership will establish a protected computing environment combining local AI processing and secure cloud infrastructure, supporting cybersecurity and safeguarding sensitive industrial data while accelerating robotics adoption across its shipbuilding operations.
